Catching Bugs Before They Land: JiTTesting’s Human-on-the-Loop Approach at Full Scale
abstract: Over the last year we’ve been sharing our work leveraging large language models to catch bugs on the fly — a novel approach we call Catching Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests). Now, we’re sharing the results and positive impact we’ve seen with Catching JiTTests deployed into production. Our paper, “ Just-in-Time Catching Test Generation at Meta ,” fully details our initial deployment and testing with Catching JiTTests. Every code change improves our platform, but it also introduces new complexity. With hundreds of millions of lines of code constantly evolving at Meta, traditional testing can’t keep pace. Catching risks proactively, before code lands, enables us to identify risks earlier, respond more effectively, and deliver reliable experiences at scale. Over the last year, we’ve shared our research into applying large language models (LLMs) to generate software tests . More specifically, we’ve shared our work with Just-in-Time Tests (JiTTests) , a novel testing approach where we leverage LLMs to catch bugs on the fly, even ones that traditional testing might not catch. In the five months since we first unveiled this work, we’ve deployed our Catching JiTTests approach to determine its scalability and applicability to the wider industry. Today, Catching JiTTests are no longer a research prototype; they’re part of Meta’s infrastructure, and they’re helping our engineers catch more bugs with less load and a smaller chance of false positives. The Advantage of Catching JiTTests Most AI-based approaches to preventing bugs in code use LLMs and/or agentic AI to review code and detect faults based on prior experience. They work through the same review process that a human reviewer would, only faster. Catching JiTTests is a fundamentally different approach (Table 1): It generates executable tests that demonstrate a concrete behavioral difference introduced by the change. While it requires more computational steps, it catches classes of bugs that LLM- or agent-based code reviews might not. Table 1. Key differences between traditional LLM-based code review and Catching JiTTests. How We Implemented Catching JiTTests at Meta JiTTests are automatically generated and designed to fail, surfacing bugs in code changes (diffs) before they land in production. When they’re applied to a codebase as large as Meta’s, one challenge is distinguishing strong catches (i.e., true-positive failures that reveal real bugs) from weak catches (i.e., tests that may be false positives). It boils down to a specific question: For every proposed diff, how can we automatically generate tests that find the most severe bugs before they cause severe issues, and do so with a high true-positive rate and without impeding the velocity of our engineers? To address this, we developed two tandem workflows: An “intent-aware” workflow that infers the intention and risks of a code change and targets test generation toward likely failure points. A “dodgy diff” workflow that treats every code change as if it were a mutant/bug and generates tests to expose its behavioral differences without reasoning about intent. It implicitly asserts that a diff is buggy (hence the term “dodgy”). Figure 1. The architecture of the dodgy diff and intent-aware workflows for Catching JiTTests. To filter false positives, we employed a traditional rule-based approach combined with an ensemble approach we call “LLM-as-Judge,” which aggregates judgements from several state-of-the-art (SOTA) LLMs, all tasked with classifying weak catches as likely true or false positives. We also maintained human review, with an eye toward reducing review load. Our goal is to maintain the consistency of human labeling but reduce the likelihood of an engineer being brought in to review a weak catch. title: Meta Andromeda: Powering the Next Generation of Ads Retrieval Through Model-System Co-Design
abstract: This post describes the next generation of Meta Andromeda, Meta’s personalized ads retrieval engine, and how co-designing the model, system, and GPU hardware unlocks a new efficiency frontier for ads retrieval. In production, the system scores every eligible ad with near ranking-level model performance at retrieval scale and surfaces the top candidates at over one billion ads per second, a new throughput benchmark for ads retrieval-stage models (i.e., a 100x lift compared to the 2024 Meta Andromeda system). For advertisers, this means better performance automatically from the retrieval system matching ads across a larger candidate pool, within the same latency budget. Since 2025, Meta Andromeda has delivered a 2.4% increase in conversions on Facebook. Meta Andromeda is Meta’s machine learning system for personalized ads retrieval, the first stage of the ads recommendation pipeline. Retrieval narrows a vast pool of eligible ads down to a small set of strong candidates in milliseconds; a later, more computationally expensive ranking stage then scores those survivors in fine detail. Historically, the deep modeling quality of the ranking stage has been too costly to apply at retrieval’s scale. Building on the retrieval foundation established with Andromeda’s 2024 launch on the NVIDIA GH200 Grace Hopper Superchip, this post shares how co-designing the model, system, and hardware together brings near ranking-level performance to the retrieval scale. Challenges and Opportunities in Scaling Retrieval The 2024 Andromeda deployment reimplemented retrieval with an end-to-end optimized retrieval implementation from custom AI hardware with hierarchical indexing and GPU-native operators to a purpose-built ML model, growing model capacity by four orders of magnitude. Since then, generative AI creative tools have helped advertisers rapidly create hundreds of millions of new ads, growing Meta’s ads candidate pool to an unprecedented scale. Scoring such a large ad candidate pool with a more accurate model at a much higher system throughput requires fundamental technology breakthroughs in model quality, system architecture, and hardware utilization jointly. Higher Model Performance Requires a New Architecture Ads retrieval has an outsized ROI on incremental quality: Small improvements in retrieval model performance can drive large gains in advertiser value. The rapid expansion of our ads candidate pool makes optimizing for hardware capacity ROI an increasingly critical factor. The 2024 Meta Andromeda retrieval models have established a highly effective foundation with their GPU-optimized deep neural network architecture. To keep improving retrieval performance at a sustainable compute cost at our current scale, however, we must move beyond that paradigm. This requires a fundamental architectural evolution to push model performance boundaries significantly without a proportional increase in costs. New System Bottlenecks at Billion Scale The 2024 Meta Andromeda system evaluates at tens of millions of ads per second per GPU card. Meeting the new business demand requires a throughput at multi-billion ads evaluated per second per card in the system. At billions of ads per second throughput, the memory bandwidth of passing ad tensors through memory hierarchy becomes the new bottleneck. Intermediate tensors between GPU kernels account for terabytes per second of memory traffic, and shipping ads between local CPU hosts and remote hardware accelerators evaluating models saturates the network link. This requires a new system co-design that unifies these fragmented, distributed workloads into a single GPU pipeline. Pushing Towards the Hardware Limits With retrieval running on GPU, the important optimization question is “How close are we to the hardware ceiling, and how much room remains for future model growth?” Answering this requires pushing each component of the retrieval pipeline to the limits of the current hardware generation, a challenge that motiva

title: From synthetic enterprise data evaluations to real Microsoft Copilot AI confidence
abstract: At a glance Evaluating Microsoft Copilot at enterprise scale requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations, yet real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. To resolve this tension, we built Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform: full-scale synthetic enterprise environments grounded in publicly available real-world data sources such as O*NET occupational data, online job postings, and SEC filings. The synthetic environments mimic real business workflows, helping Microsoft find issues that generic benchmarks would miss. Safety and privacy are built into the platform by design. Every environment is fully synthetic and automated content-safety checks keep the generated data free of harmful or personally identifiable material. Every day, millions of knowledge workers around the world rely on Microsoft Copilot to draft documents, summarize meetings, surface relevant information, and accelerate productivity. Behind the scenes, this is powered by a network of AI systems, and ensuring they work as intended requires a thoughtful approach to evaluation. At Microsoft, we know that high performance doesn’t come from guesswork. It comes from testing, measuring, and iterating constantly. Healthcare organizations are constantly synthesizing safety signals from across teams so that they can make faster, better decisions that directly influence patient outcomes and regulatory confidence. They may ask Copilot to summarize a meeting and extract action items for their teams. Within seconds, Copilot delivers a structured summary citing specific discussion points from the transcript. But how do we ensure this response is accurate, complete, and properly grounded in the meeting content? This is where our evaluation system comes in. We’ve developed a structured evaluation strategy called Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform , which includes industry specific evaluation datasets designed to test AI systems against realistic enterprise scenarios, grounded in three core pillars: Synthetic enterprise environments : simulated Microsoft Copilot environments with realistic users, meetings, emails, documents, and organizational structures that replicate the complexity of real organizations without using any customer data Automated query generation pipelines for rapid, reproducible creation of evaluation datasets Structured quality frameworks to ensure synthetic data meets the bar for meaningful evaluation Figure 1: Components of Industry Evaluation Data Generation Platform Together, these pillars help us answer two fundamental questions: Is Microsoft Copilot actually doing what our users need it to do, and can we prove it without ever touching their data ? In this blog post, we’ll walk through our evaluation system and processes, from synthetic environment generation to automated query pipelines, and how it all comes together to establish the first standardized evaluation baseline for Microsoft Copilot. Synthetic enterprise environments Evaluating enterprise AI requires test data that captures the full complexity of real organizations: reporting structures, project histories, communication patterns, and domain specific workflows. But real enterprise data contains sensitive information that cannot be used for evaluation under any circumstances. This is the central tension we set out to resolve. Rather than relying on small, manually curated test fixtures, we generate full scale synthetic environments : simulated enterprise workspaces, each with realistic organizational structures, communication histories, and work artifacts. In Microsoft terminology, each of these simulated workspaces is called a “tenant”. A tenant is an isolated organizational environment with its own users, data, and configurations. In this edition of Microsoft Research Focus , host Sowbhagya Suresh shares some of the latest news and cutting-edge research from across Microsoft—from understanding the challenges facing coding agents to uncovering how people use AI at work and improving extended-range weather forecasting. Catch up on the ideas, tools, and discoveries researchers are exploring today and get a quick look at what’s coming next. title: Speeding up language models for travel applications
abstract: Travel platforms serve millions of daily users by answering questions about destinations, offering hotel recommendations, and helping users plan their trips. In recent years, many platforms have turned to large language models (LLMs) to improve these services. The LLMs give accurate, contextually relevant travel advice thanks to their size: they typically have tens of billions of parameters. Unfortunately, such large models are also computationally expensive, and that expense scales with the number of customer queries. What’s more, such large models can be too slow for web and mobile applications, where a delay of even 100 milliseconds can cost a company customers and revenue. To address these scaling and latency challenges, we explored two complementary optimization techniques. One is a compression technique known as knowledge distillation (KD), in which a slow but powerful model produces training targets for a faster, lightweight model. The other, called Medusa, is a framework that transforms sequential next-token predictions — a common bottleneck in LLMs — into parallel computations. Working with leading online travel agency Booking.com, we applied KD and Medusa techniques to the LLMs that power various aspects of its user experience, looking to improve either latency or cost effectiveness. We focused on three features in particular: The AI Trip Planner: A conversational assistant that must extract travel preferences from dialogue in less than a second (latency); Smart Filters: A feature that converts natural-language search queries into structured information filters in real time (latency); Accommodation Description Generation: A feature that produces property descriptions on the scale of millions of listings (cost effectiveness). We demonstrated that combining both KD and Medusa maintains the quality of the best open-source LLMs at less than one-third the cost while running up to 20 times as fast. Our framework ensures that travel platforms or other applications that rely on LLMs can deliver fast, cost-effective, accurate responses in real-world scenarios. We presented these techniques at last year’s meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (ACL), where it received the Industry Track best-paper award. Our approach: Medusa plus knowledge distillation Medusa is a framework designed to reduce LLM latency in real-time applications such as chat and code generation. It improves computational efficiency at run time — inference time — rather than during training. Ordinarily, an LLM generates text one token — word or word part — at a time. Medusa accelerates this process by predicting multiple tokens in parallel. Medusa does this by adding prediction modules, called Medusa heads, to the base LLM, one head for each token decoded in parallel. GPU hardware that LLMs run on is optimized for parallelism, so it can handle parallel token decoding with little additional overhead. Medusa offers significant speedups, typically two- to fourfold without compromising generation quality. Knowledge distillation addresses the deployment challenges of large, parameter-heavy models by transferring knowledge from larger “teacher” models to smaller “student” models. Typically, a teacher model is first trained or fine-tuned on high-quality labeled data, then used to generate predictions on additional unlabeled data. The manually labeled and machine-labeled data are then combined to train a smaller student model, which learns to mimic the teacher’s behavior. The student model retains much of the teacher’s performance but is significantly more efficient, making it better suited for real-world scenarios such as high-volume consumer-facing websites. In our work, we integrate KD and Medusa in a unified pipeline starting with pretrained base models. title: Managing Amazon Bedrock costs end to end: A playbook for FinOps and platform teams
abstract: Cost management for generative AI is a shared responsibility between the teams that build applications and the teams accountable for cloud spend. Many teams start by comparing per-model token rates and asking application teams to shorten prompts. Those steps help, but they don’t answer the questions that finance and engineering leaders ask as usage scales: which team spent this, on which workload, and was that spend inside an approved budget? Agentic workloads make those questions more pressing. A conversational assistant typically issues one model invocation per user turn. An agentic workflow, such as an AI coding assistant that plans a change, reads files, calls tools, and iterates, issues many invocations per task and carries a larger context on each one. Token consumption therefore scales with the degree of autonomy you grant the workflow and the size of the context it carries, rather than with the number of user interactions. Because consumption is a function of how a workload is designed and operated, cost management for generative AI is an architectural and operational discipline. Published averages are a poor substitute for your own numbers: use the AWS Pricing Calculator and the Amazon Bedrock pricing page to model rates, and use Step 2 of this post to measure what your workloads actually consume. The fix isn’t a cheaper model or a smaller prompt. It’s an operating model: a repeatable loop that attributes every dollar to an owner, makes every request observable, alerts on and enforces budgets before overspend compounds, optimizes the platform defaults that drive most waste, and reviews the whole system on a cadence. In this post, you learn how to manage Amazon Bedrock cost in five steps. You attribute every dollar to an owner, make every request observable, control spend with budgets and enforcement, optimize the platform defaults that drive most avoidable spend, and operate a review cadence that turns data into decisions. This approach is built from AWS building blocks, and you can customize it and apply it to your own environment. The post is written for two audiences: FinOps practitioners who own attribution, chargeback, budgets, and anomaly review, and platform engineering teams who own logging, request metadata, enforcement, and routing defaults. The operating model in one view Five stages, run as a loop. Attribute: every Amazon Bedrock dollar lands on an identity, team, and application in the billing pipeline. Observe: every request is logged with enough metadata to explain what generated the spend. Enforce: budgets have teeth, with alerts at minimum and hard blocks where the risk demands them. Optimize: the platform defaults (model routing, caching, token limits) remove waste centrally instead of asking every team to be careful. Operate: a small scorecard and a review cadence turn the data into decisions. FinOps leads stages one and five. Platform engineering leads two through four. The review is joint. The stages are sequenced deliberately. Each one depends on the ones before it, and teams that jump straight to optimization without attribution and observability are guessing. Figure 1: The five-stage operating model, run as a continuous loop Stage 1: Attribute every dollar You can’t manage what you can’t attribute, and everything downstream (chargeback, budgets, enforcement, anomaly detection) depends on this stage. The foundation is the granular cost attribution of Amazon Bedrock (see Introducing granular cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock ): Amazon Bedrock automatically attributes inference costs to the AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) principal that made the call, across all models, with no resources to manage. The caller’s ARN lands in the line_item_iam_principal column of the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) 2.0 , and coverage spans IAM users, roles, federated identities, and API keys. title: Preview web apps live as your coding agent builds them with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore runtime
abstract: Coding agents now build working web apps: a dashboard, a product page, a prototype that a product team wants to try. The fastest way to review that work is to open the app, use it, ask for a change, and check the result. That loop works well when the app keeps running where the agent edits it, so each change shows up in the browser within seconds. When the app must be copied out and deployed somewhere else first, every change waits for a deployment, and the review slows down to that pace. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is a platform to build, connect, and optimize agents at scale, with your choice of agent framework and foundation model (FM). AgentCore runtime , a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, runs each agent session in its own isolated microVM. With Session endpoints , you can open an app running in that session from your own browser. Session Endpoints give each session an authenticated URL that forwards each request’s HTTP method, path, query string, and body, and WebSocket connections, to the ports you allow. You can watch the page update as the agent saves each file. In this post, you deploy a coding agent that keeps a Vite website running in its session, then open one local page with a chat on the left and the live website on the right. You ask the agent to switch the site to a dark color theme, follow its steps as they stream in, and watch the website change without a refresh. Finally, you look at what happens internally: a second port in the same session, and the requests the Session endpoint refuses. The complete sample, including the notebook this post follows, is in the 14-remote-access folder of the agentcore-samples GitHub repo . How Session endpoints work Each session gets its own Session endpoint, and six details shape how you use it. You choose which ports it reaches. You set allowedPorts when you call CreateAgentRuntime : 1–5 entries, each a single port or a range within 8000–12000, excluding the reserved platform ports . Allowing a port doesn’t start a server, so your application must listen on it, bound to 0.0.0.0 . The URL arrives with the session. The InvokeAgentRuntime response carries it in the X-Amzn-Bedrock-AgentCore-Runtime-Session-Endpoint-Url header, which SDKs that model it expose as sessionEndpointUrl . Every request is authenticated. For a runtime that uses AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) , each HTTP request, HTTP/2 stream, and WebSocket handshake carries a Signature Version 4 (SigV4) signature. The caller also needs bedrock-agentcore:InvokeAgentRuntimeProxy on the runtime and its runtime endpoint. For a runtime with an inbound JSON Web Token (JWT) authorizer , each request carries a bearer token instead. Knowing the URL doesn’t grant access. The host name selects the port. Your client connects on port 443 regardless of the target port, and a prefix on the host name chooses the port inside the session: https://8090--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/index.html https://8081--<session-endpoint-id>.runtime.bedrock-agentcore.<region>.on.aws/status It carries the protocols your server speaks. HTTP/1.1 and HTTP/2 requests, including server-sent events and gRPC, and WebSocket connections all pass through. This walkthrough uses HTTP/1.1 and WebSocket. It’s scoped to one session. The URL needs credentials on every request and lasts only as long as the session, so use it to build, test, and review what your agent produces. To serve an app to your users, deploy it to a hosting service such as AWS Amplify Hosting . A browser can’t add a SigV4 signature or a bearer token to the requests a page makes on its own, so the Session endpoint client in the bedrock-agentcore SDK can open a local endpoint on your machine. Your browser opens http://localhost:8088 , and the local endpoint adds your credentials to each request and WebSocket handshake before forwarding it. title: How Worldwide Express automated freight exceptions with Amazon Bedrock
abstract: Worldwide Express (part of ShipStation Global) had built something big: approximately $5 billion in systemwide revenue, over 75 less-than-truckload (LTL) carriers and more than 130,000 customers. But that same scale had a hidden cost. Every month, $15 million in free cash flow sat frozen, locked in billing exceptions no one had resolved yet. Each one had to be chased down by hand, carrier by carrier, with its own rules to check. Worldwide Express outsourced to a team that worked cases one at a time, calling customers and carriers for each dispute. The exceptions piled up, cash stayed stuck, and every order took longer to turn into money. Worldwide Express worked with AWS and LTM to build a multi-agentic AI solution with Amazon Bedrock that plugs directly into their transportation management system (TMS), SpeedShip. Six months after launch, the company reported a 75 percent reduction in active exceptions, a 4-week improvement in time-to-cash, $1M annual savings, and a one-time $10M free cash flow infusion. In this post, we describe the challenge, explain how Worldwide Express designed the multi-agent solution, and share the results. The challenge In LTL freight, roughly 14 percent of invoices fail the standard three-way match between the purchase order, the goods receipt, and the carrier invoice. When a match fails, the invoice enters exception handling. For Worldwide Express, exceptions fell into three categories: Line-item mismatches: Quantities or service codes that didn’t align with the shipment record. Pricing variances: The carrier billed a rate different from the contracted price. Unexpected accessorial charges: Liftgate fees, residential surcharges, or reweigh adjustments that weren’t on the original quote. Each exception triggered a five-step manual process: Identify the exception type by cross-referencing the invoice against the purchase order, goods receipt, and pricing. Research the root cause in vendor records. Send email to the carrier or warehouse with dispute details. Wait for a response. Execute the resolution in the TMS. With each carrier operating under its own tariff structure and dispute workflow, this process consumed most of the FinOps team’s bandwidth. Rule-based process automation (RPA) can handle structured, predictable workflows. However, exception resolution requires contextual judgment: interpreting a carrier’s accessorial policy, comparing charges against shipment data, and deciding validity given a carrier, exception type, and dollar amount. That variability is what made the problem a fit for the agentic AI framework. From assessment to production In June 2025, Worldwide Express engaged the AWS Business Transformation & Value Advisory team to identify 19 automation opportunities across the Order-to-Cash lifecycle. Knowing the business value of exceptions automation, Worldwide Express moved from assessment to production in less than 6 months. How it works The solution runs on AWS. Amazon Bedrock provides AI reasoning, and Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2) is the engine. The design calls for fine-grained control over how each agent reasons, where decision boundaries sit, and how exceptions are routed between agents. Building the framework directly on Amazon EC2, with Amazon Bedrock providing inference, keeps that orchestration logic fully in the team’s hands and supports open source agent libraries. Production controls of business logic make each agent’s role, inputs, and decision boundaries explicit and auditable. In a billing-dispute workflow, every automated decision needs to be explainable. Agents When an invoice exception is detected, the system routes it to one of three specialized AI agents, each handling a specific type of billing dispute: Invoice Matching Agent finds the matching shipment record and flags what doesn’t line up. Pricing Variance Agent compares the carrier’s charge against the contracted rate and determines whether the difference is valid. Accessorial Validation Agent

title: Configure the ChatGPT desktop app with Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US)
abstract: The ChatGPT desktop app is now available on Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US) , providing access to OpenAI’s frontier models through two components. Work completes complex, multi-step tasks and delivers review-ready results, and Codex is a coding agent for developing, testing, and reviewing software. This walkthrough is intended for organizations whose security architecture requires model inference to use AWS GovCloud (US) identities, endpoints, and Regional controls. It configures Codex to route model requests through Amazon Bedrock Mantle in us-gov-west-1 , where access can be governed using AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM) and existing AWS GovCloud (US) network controls. Codex is the OpenAI coding agent for AI-powered software development. With GPT models powering inference, Codex introduces a new class of intelligence optimized for complex, long-horizon developer workflows. You can use the ChatGPT desktop app, the Codex CLI, and IDE integrations with Visual Studio Code, JetBrains, and Xcode. Model inference is routed through the Responses API on Amazon Bedrock. For customers with data residency requirements, processing stays within the Amazon Bedrock AWS Region that you select. You pay per token with no seat licenses and no per-developer commitments. Zero data retention (ZDR) is also supported. In this configurable mode, prompts and responses are processed without being written to durable storage by AWS or shared with model providers. This helps you protect sensitive information and meet stringent data-governance, privacy, and security requirements. This post walks through a controlled local deployment of the ChatGPT desktop app that sends model inference to Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US-West). The configuration uses API-mode sign-in, a managed device policy, a named AWS profile, and network restrictions. These restrictions allow access only to the approved Amazon Bedrock endpoint while disabling other external connections and network-enabled capabilities. The result is a deployment that an agency security team can test and document before approving broader use. Using AWS GovCloud (US) and following this guide do not, by themselves, authorize your workload. Your organization remains responsible for reviewing the selected model, AWS services, Region, endpoint, workstation controls, repositories, credentials, and data flows against its system security plan and authorization process. Solution overview You can use the ChatGPT desktop app in two ways: Work for larger tasks that need planning, research, files, and a finished result. Codex for technical work such as editing code, running tests, and reviewing pull requests. The ChatGPT desktop app runs on an organization-managed computer through the desktop app or CLI. It uses the configured AWS credentials to securely send requests to the Amazon Bedrock Mantle endpoint in us-gov-west-1 . Because this setup uses AWS directly, ChatGPT workspace rules and user roles don’t control it. The main security controls are the computer’s policies and the AWS identity and permissions being used. Walkthrough The configuration has three main steps: set up authentication, set up the ChatGPT desktop app configuration files, and then launch, initialize, and verify the deployment. Prerequisites Before setting up the ChatGPT desktop app with AWS GovCloud (US), make sure your version of the ChatGPT desktop app supports Amazon Bedrock in AWS GovCloud (US). You need an approved AWS GovCloud (US) account, an IAM identity and approved credentials, access to the approved model, AWS Region, and endpoint, and permission to use them. You also need to set up the requirements.toml and config.toml files. Step 1: Set up authentication Select the approved AWS GovCloud (US) account and IAM identity or role with access to the approved model in us-gov-west-1 . title: How the UK Amazon Quick User Group grew in 2026
abstract: The Amazon Quick User Group – United Kingdom is a community of Amazon Quick users in the United Kingdom who meet quarterly to exchange knowledge, share best practices, learn through hands-on sessions, and discuss their experiences using the service. These user groups function as collaborative forums where members learn, connect, and innovate together. Whether you’re already using Amazon Quick or just getting started, we’d love for you to join the UK Amazon Quick User Group and become part of a growing community that’s redefining how organizations make decisions with data. In this post, we’re thrilled to share our 2026 yearly roundup, highlighting all three quarterly meetups that have taken place since the group’s launch and the momentum that has followed. The events drew more than 150 attendees, and the energy in the room, fueled by agentic AI and the potential of Amazon Quick, was clear. Across industries, customers are using Amazon Quick to turn data chaos into faster decisions, higher satisfaction, and scalable growth. Their work spans real-time incident management, eliminating dashboard sprawl with governed data layers, and automating most support workflows with AI. Why Amazon Quick user groups matter The UK Amazon Quick User Group is a local community of Amazon Quick users who come together quarterly to share knowledge, best practices, and experiences with the service. Amazon Quick user groups serve as collaborative forums where members can: Learn and share – Exchange real-world insights about the capabilities of Amazon Quick, from interactive dashboards and data storytelling to agentic AI-powered automations and custom agents. title: Building intent-driven UI testing with Amazon Nova Act
abstract: To scale intent-driven UI testing across its product teams, Epsilon , a data, technology, and marketing-services company and part of Publicis Groupe , turned to Amazon Nova Act . With hundreds of millions of consumer profiles and thousands of brand relationships, Epsilon needed UI testing that could keep pace with rapid application changes. The solution could not create maintenance overhead for every product team. Within Epsilon, the Agentic Platform team (50 engineers) builds shared infrastructure so other product teams can build, deploy, govern, and run AI agents safely. With this shared platform, teams get a skills-based agent builder. They also get federated identity and pre-flight authorization, Model Context Protocol (MCP) integration, and cross-account provisioning. When a product team wants to adopt AI tooling, they get capabilities without additional configuration and without re-solving identity, security, browser infrastructure, or model integration on their own. One of those managed capabilities is UI testing . With Amazon Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Epsilon’s platform team could deliver resilient, intent-driven testing as a service to teams on the platform. In this post, we walk through Epsilon’s architecture for delivering UI testing as a managed platform service, show the core Nova Act and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool integration code, highlight a concrete 18-step test workflow, and share best practices and measured results. The challenge: Enhancing coverage, not replacing what works Epsilon’s existing UI testing practice was not broken. The team maintained a Playwright-based regression suite that validated functionality across their web applications, and it worked well. Playwright remains their regression backbone today. The opportunity Epsilon identified was additive, not corrective: Scripted Playwright tests are effective for deterministic regression checks. However, they are tightly coupled to selectors and page structure. Cosmetic UI changes can break them even when the underlying functionality is sound. Multiple product teams needed full testing coverage against their own applications. Standing up browser infrastructure, managing dependencies, and integrating with identity systems per team created duplicative effort. The platform team wanted UI testing to be a managed capability that fit their existing agent model, not a custom CLI that every onboarded team had to operate. The goal: layer intent-based testing on top of the existing Playwright regression suite. Deliver it as a multi-tenant platform service so that each Epsilon product team could consume through the same API surface they used for every other agent capability. Why Epsilon chose Amazon Nova Act and the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool Epsilon evaluated options against two requirements: natural-language test authoring (to complement selector-based Playwright tests) and managed browser infrastructure (to fit their multi-tenant platform model). With Amazon Nova Act combined with Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, Epsilon could address both. Natural-language steps. Test steps are plain-English instructions executed by Nova Act. They are resilient to cosmetic UI changes and readable by non-engineers. A step like “Confirm the rewards balance is visible” ages far better than a brittle CSS selector. AWS managed, ephemeral browser sessions. With Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool, teams get isolated browser instances with no binaries to ship and no display server to maintain. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Browser Tool also offers live view for human observation or takeover (useful for CAPTCHAs or multi-factor authentication), session recording to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3), and AWS CloudTrail audit, all without additional configuration. title: Build a repeatable PHP-to-Java migration engine with Kiro
abstract: When your team moves a mature PHP application to Java, you gain stronger type safety, broader library support, and more predictable scaling. A PHP codebase built over the years with Laravel, Symfony, or Doctrine carries business rules in places that are not obvious, from Eloquent traits to XML mapping files, so a structurally similar Java port can compile cleanly and still behave differently. This post shows how to turn PHP-to-Java migration from a one-time leap of faith into a measurable, repeatable process using Kiro . Kiro is an AI integrated development environment (IDE) that pairs an AI agent with your codebase to run multi-step engineering tasks with you in the loop. The approach centers on a reusable engine: a shared methodology, a mechanical discovery scanner, and an eight-phase workflow. This engine treats the original PHP application as the specification and refuses to declare the Java port correct until a parity harness verifies it. Prerequisites Before getting started, you need: Familiarity with PHP (Laravel/Eloquent or Symfony/Doctrine). Java knowledge (Spring Boot, JPA) helps you review the generated output, but the engine produces idiomatic Java for you, so you don’t need to rewrite the application in Java yourself. A Kiro workspace with access to Skills and Steering files. PHP 8.0 or newer on the machine running the discovery scanner, and Java 21 with Maven for the generated Spring Boot projects. A basic understanding of migration planning (discovery, translation, and validation). What you will learn in this post You start with an open repository, so you can run the engine yourself rather than read about it. Everything the engine knows lives in a small set of skill files, and with those files, you can run the same methodology in more than one way. Two ways to run the engine: Kiro and AWS Transform Everything here is packaged as skill files: versioned Markdown capability packages that encode the migration methodology (php-to-java-migration) and the discovery scanner workflow (php-model-discovery). Because that knowledge lives in files rather than any one tool, you can run the same methodology in two ways. Method 1: Kiro, interactive and developer-in-the-loop Kiro brings an AI agent into your editor to drive a migration step by step. Open the repository root as a Kiro workspace and the skills activate automatically when you ask Kiro to migrate a PHP application. Kiro then walks the eight-phase workflow with explicit approval gates, so you review the discovery manifest, approve the rulebook, and sign off on each phase before the next begins. It’s the mode used for every example in this post. Method 2: AWS Transform, agentic and at portfolio scale AWS Transform is the AWS agentic AI service for large-scale migration and modernization, and it now integrates natively with Kiro. Through that integration, you can hand AWS Transform the same skill files that govern an interactive Kiro session, so discovery before translation, the parity harness as referee, and ‘ fix the loop, not the code ’ apply to an autonomous run. When each path fits Control and autonomy: Use Kiro to work through the code first: run the skill on one application, read the generated Java, and run the tests. When you want to migrate more, AWS Transform runs the same methodology agentically with review at the checkpoints the skill defines. Scale and novelty: Kiro handles one application at a time and suits first-of-a-kind frameworks. AWS Transform runs many applications as parallel jobs. A shared feedback loop: Both paths read the same skill files, so every rulebook fix made in Kiro improves the next AWS Transform run, and vice versa. Solution overview: One shared brain, many projects The engine is organized around a single principle: one shared brain, many projects. title: Lend and borrow resources across teams with AWS Batch’s quota management for SageMaker Training jobs
abstract: With the launch of AWS Batch support for Amazon SageMaker Training jobs, customers gained a new fully managed way to queue, schedule, and retry machine learning (ML) training workloads without building their own infrastructure. Instead, they use the queuing and scheduling features of AWS Batch. As organizations scale their artificial intelligence and machine learning (AI/ML) operations and onboard more teams, coordinating access to shared graphics processing unit (GPU) capacity can introduce additional communication, coordination, and configuration overhead for administrators. This overhead includes setting up separate queues, adjusting capacity limits, and carefully orchestrating the right workloads to get the right resources at the right time. A core value proposition of AWS Batch is helping customers increase utilization of their compute, and as training environments grow, so does the opportunity to do more with existing capacity. Working backward from customers managing multi-team training environments, we heard a consistent request: give us a way to define allocations per team or project, share idle capacity automatically, and run our highest-priority workloads first. This request led us to build quota management , a new scheduling capability for AWS Batch. Administrators can use it to divide compute capacity into quota shares, organized by team, project, or workload. Each quota share uses configurable resource-sharing strategies that maximize GPU utilization while honoring each team’s allocation when it matters most. This post shows how quota management works, including how to configure quota shares with lending and borrowing strategies, set up in-share preemption for priority workloads, and get started using the SageMaker Python SDK. Quota shares and preemption Administrators can allocate and share constrained GPU resources by defining a quota share for separate entities, such as individual teams or projects. Each quota share includes compute quotas (capacity limits) and resource-sharing strategies for idle compute. These strategies determine whether idle compute is reserved until jobs arrive ( RESERVE ), lent to other quota shares that have work available ( LEND ), or both lent when idle and borrowed when the share has work that might benefit ( LEND_AND_BORROW ). A quota share operates as a virtual queue nested hierarchically within an associated job queue. When scheduling jobs for a job queue, AWS Batch prioritizes quota shares that are under their capacity limits as it iterates through the associated quota shares. If jobs arrive in a quota share that has lent out its capacity, AWS Batch performs cross-share preemption. This reclaims resources for the lending quota share, so administrators don’t need to track down the jobs borrowing capacity and terminate them on their own. If jobs arrive in a quota share that is at or above its capacity limit, AWS Batch checks whether there’s available capacity to borrow from another quota share. If so, workloads can run using otherwise-idle capacity. You can turn on priority-based in-share preemption when you configure a quota share. Where cross-share preemption reclaims lent capacity as jobs arrive in a lending quota share, in-share preemption preempts lower priority jobs that are in the SCHEDULED, STARTING, or RUNNING state. This allows higher priority jobs at the front of the queue to start running sooner. For this example, see the sample IAM permissions needed to invoke AWS Batch and SageMaker APIs. The example uses the SageMaker Python SDK v3. title: How MoEngage turned over 400 APIs into agent tools with AgentCore Gateway
abstract: This post was co-written with Nikhil Kumar and Shakir Khan from MoEngage. When engineering teams start building AI agents, the capabilities those agents need usually already exist as internal APIs. Campaign creation, segment queries, delivery stats. The challenge isn’t building new functionality. The challenge is making hundreds of private APIs safely reachable by agents without exposing them to the public internet, without giving models control over identity, and without flooding context windows with hundreds of tool definitions. MoEngage, the agentic customer engagement platform that more than 1,350 consumer brands use to deliver personalized experiences across push, email, in-app, SMS, WhatsApp, and RCS, faced exactly this problem. Behind the product sit roughly 400 internal REST APIs, built by 25 engineering teams, running in private virtual private clouds (VPCs) across seven AWS Regions. MoEngage isolates these APIs regionally to meet data residency commitments and doesn’t expose them to the public internet. The capability the agents needed was already running in production. Making it reachable, safely, was the hard part. In this post, we walk through how MoEngage used AgentCore Gateway, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, to turn those private APIs into permission-scoped agent tools. The approach saved MoEngage an estimated six months of platform engineering effort, and onboarding a new API now takes hours instead of days. No product team wrote Model Context Protocol (MCP) server code, no networking was provisioned per integration, and no public endpoint exists anywhere in the path. Why 20 MCP servers was the wrong answer The Model Context Protocol (MCP) gives agents a standard way to discover and call tools. The straightforward path to adopting it is for each team to expose its own MCP server. MoEngage costed that out and rejected it. Over 20 MCP servers means over 20 deployments to monitor, patch, and keep protocol-compatible as MCP evolves. Cross-domain agents, the useful ones that read a campaign, check its segment, and inspect delivery stats, would need to connect to several servers and reconcile them. And every team would need MCP expertise unrelated to its actual product work. So MoEngage established the principle that shaped everything that followed: Individual engineering teams do not implement MCP. Teams build REST APIs and declare which operations should be tools. The AI Platform team owns the MCP layer end to end. A team’s responsibility ends at a well-described OpenAPI spec. That principle immediately created three requirements: a central tool surface that agents connect to once rather than per-service, per-agent authorization enforced server-side rather than by convention, and private connectivity that does not need to be rebuilt for every new API. Building all of this from scratch was an option. A custom central MCP server would solve the 20-servers problem but leave MoEngage building a tool-generation pipeline, a policy file format, a tool-alias registry for renames, and circuit breakers. All custom code, all owned by one team, all of it undifferentiated work that does not make MoEngage’s agents smarter or its customers’ campaigns better. Four constraints that shaped the architecture Before evaluating any solution, MoEngage defined four constraints. All four had to be met simultaneously. A solution that addressed two but broke the third and fourth was not viable. Nothing gets a public endpoint. MoEngage’s internal APIs are VPC-private by policy. Any solution that required exposing them, even behind additional authentication, was a non-starter. The conventional workaround is per-integration networking: a NAT gateway here, a reverse proxy there, a VPN tunnel for the third one. Multiply that by seven Regions and the operational surface grows faster than the set of agents does. title: Accelerate agentic AI with NVIDIA Nemotron models on Amazon EKS and SageMaker HyperPod EKS
abstract: NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL joins the NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano , Nano Omni , Super , Ultra , and Nemotron 3.5 Lightning models already available on AWS. It’s a 120B-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) model that activates 12B parameters per token. It combines reasoning and tool use with text, image, document, and video understanding, so one model serves both text and visual tasks. This post explores its architecture and use cases, then shows how to deploy it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) , Amazon EKS Auto Mode , and Amazon SageMaker HyperPod EKS . About Nemotron 3.5 Super VL NVIDIA Nemotron 3.5 Super VL is an open multimodal model distilled from Nemotron 3 Ultra. NVIDIA publishes the weights, training datasets, and post-training recipes, so you can customize the model for domain-specific workloads and run it on infrastructure you control. Model details: 120B total parameters, 12B active per token. Hybrid Mamba-2, MoE , and attention layers with a RADIO vision encoder. Context length up to 1M tokens. Input: text, image, document, and video. Output: text. BF16 and NVFP4 checkpoints. NVIDIA reports 63.44 percent on Hermes Bench and 87.05 percent on LangChain agent evaluations, and 80.8 percent on the CharXiv chart-reasoning benchmark. ( technical report ) Model architecture Nemotron 3.5 Super VL uses a hybrid Mamba-Transformer MoE architecture, interleaving Mamba-2, attention, and expert layers. Sparse routing activates 12B of the 120B parameters per token, so compute per token matches a much smaller model while GPU memory still holds the full weights. Mamba-2 layers carry a constant-size state during generation, so their memory does not grow with sequence length the way KV cache does, which keeps long contexts affordable. A recursively shared Multi-Token Prediction (MTP) head supports native speculative decoding. Use cases Nemotron 3.5 Super VL supports agent workflows that combine reasoning with visual understanding: Coding: test and validate code, analyze errors, recommend fixes. Web research: cross-reference and verify sources returned by search tools. Document intelligence: read tables, charts, and page layouts to produce summaries. Cyber security: identify vulnerabilities and triage threats. Video understanding: search, content, review, and incident analysis. Nemotron 3.5 Super VL integrates with major open agent frameworks and orchestration systems through NVIDIA reference implementations, cookbooks, and the NVIDIA Agent Toolkit . For the full list of supported frameworks, see the NVIDIA developer blog . Minimum GPU configurations vLLM (GPU Model / min count) BF16 NVFP4 B200/GB200 8 2 B300/GB300 4 1 H200 8 4 H100 16 8 Deployment on AWS This section gives an overview of architecture, validation, and performance evaluation approaches. A detailed walkthrough of deploying Nemotron 3.5 Super VL and Nemotron 3 Ultra on AWS is available in the aws-do-eks project, including prerequisites, cluster creation, model weights download, deployment, testing, benchmarking, and cleanup. The same pattern can also be applied to other models in the NVIDIA Nemotron family. Deployment architecture The reference implementation runs on standard Amazon EKS, EKS Auto Mode, and SageMaker HyperPod EKS. With EKS Auto Mode, AWS manages scaling, GPU, and EFA support in the cluster on your behalf. The Kubernetes manifests for model deployment are the same for each of the orchestrator options. Each cluster has a control plane hosting the Kubernetes API and a data plane of CPU and GPU nodes. CPU nodes run system and test pods, while the GPU nodes run the model. Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) stores the container images, a shared Amazon FSx for Lustre volume holds the model weights, and Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) connects the GPU nodes. title: Building an Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
abstract: If you’ve tried to get an agent into production, the model and tool use are not the blocker. The main bottleneck is everything around them: how many teams can build within a secure environment, which team owns each model and tool, how AgentOps and error handling stay inside a pre-defined boundary, and how platform, Workstream, and finance teams see cost and health across accounts. For a Platform team that wants to support many agentic use cases, that’s a platform product to design and operate. In this post, we refer to the team that manages the platform as the Platform team, and to the teams that build on it as Workstream teams. Workstream teams are the domain or product teams that build and own agents on the platform. Each Workstream team needs a paved road with approved models and tools, short-lived workload identity, isolated runtime and memory, automated evaluation, rollback, telemetry, and cost attribution. These controls need to remain consistent as Workstream teams customize prompts, tools, data access, and application behavior. When every team assembles them, controls drift, shared services become a bottleneck, and ownership is difficult to audit. In this post, we walk through the architecture and reference implementation of an enterprise Agentic AI Platform on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon Bedrock AgentCore. We cover the multi-account operating model, the Platform control plane, a repeatable per-Workstream deployment pattern, separate inference and tool gateways, and an evaluation pipeline that gates each agent before promotion to production. By the end, you should be able to deploy a governed Workstream from the companion blueprint, validate its security and lifecycle contracts, and use it as the foundation for your own agentic AI platform in the organization. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore provides modular services for building, deploying, and operating agents at scale, including runtime, gateway, identity, memory, policy, registry, and evaluations. The Enterprise Agentic AI Platform Blueprint , built on AgentCore, adds the surrounding enterprise contracts as deployable infrastructure as code: ownership, account boundaries, software delivery, observability, cost governance, and retirement. Architectural principles Before diving into the solution details, it helps to understand the organizational needs that drive the platform architecture. The common challenges we have heard from customers who establish an agent platform fall into these five categories: Governed model access: Every untrusted inference request must pass through an approved inference gateway. The gateway applies the organization’s guardrails (for example, Amazon Bedrock Guardrails or a third-party provider), restricts which models and inference AWS Regions each Workstream can use, and enforces per-Workstream rate limits, token quotas, and budgets so that no single team can exhaust shared capacity. It also carries workload identity and emits attribution data. Governed tool access: Agents must discover and invoke only approved tools through an authenticated Model Context Protocol (MCP) gateway, with exact targets, least-privilege execution roles, policy decisions, and an auditable owner. Delegated delivery: Workstream teams (for example, product teams) need to ship and roll back independently inside pre-approved boundaries, without waiting for the platform team to deploy each application or granting developers a direct infrastructure write path. Fleet operations and cost: Several personas need visibility across accounts without gaining write access to team workloads. Agent operations engineers need logs, metrics, traces, and quotas. Workstream owners need cost per agent against their budgets. FinOps and finance teams need chargeback by team or business unit through AWS Cost Explorer and the AWS Cost and Usage Report (CUR) . Security and governance leads need evidence of which workload called which model and tool. Bounded evidence and lifecycle: Every agent release

title: Distributed training with Ray Train DLCs and EFA on EKS
abstract: What usually stops PyTorch training from scaling out to a cluster is the container, not the model code. Every container needs the same CUDA runtime , a PyTorch build compiled against it, NCCL (NVIDIA Collective Communications Library), the Elastic Fabric Adapter (EFA) userspace libraries, the AWS OFI NCCL plugin that connects NCCL to EFA, and a Ray version the cluster operator agrees with. Building that image and rebuilding it each time one of those pieces moves is a project of its own, and it has nothing to do with the model you set out to train. The Ray Train Deep Learning Container (DLC) is that image, built by AWS. AWS assembles the stack, tests it as one unit, publishes it in Amazon Elastic Container Registry (Amazon ECR) Public and keeps it patched. Figure 1: One EKS cluster with a control plane managed by AWS, a CPU system node (m7i.xlarge) running the KubeRay operator and Ray head, and two EFA-enabled g6.12xlarge nodes in one Availability Zone. KubeRay builds it from one RayCluster manifest, Ray Train places eight workers, one per GPU, and inter-node collectives cross over EFA. Ray runs a job across machines as a single cluster with two roles. The Ray head coordinates and runs the global control store that tracks cluster state, the dashboard and job server you submit jobs to. Ray worker nodes supply the GPUs and run the training processes. Each worker joins the cluster by connecting to the head’s address when it starts. On Kubernetes, each of these is a pod. Kubernetes has no built-in idea of a Ray cluster, so something must create the head and worker pods, start Ray in the right role in each, point the workers at the head, and replace pods that fail. KubeRay does this. It’s an open source Kubernetes operator that adds a RayCluster resource: you describe a head group and a worker group in one manifest, and KubeRay builds and maintains the cluster from it. A single tagged image runs as both the Ray head and the Ray workers, whether KubeRay starts it on Amazon Elastic Kubernetes Service (Amazon EKS) or you start it yourself on Amazon Elastic Compute Cloud (Amazon EC2). What you add is configuration: which instances, how many GPUs each pod gets, which network transport NCCL uses, and which extra Python packages a job needs. All of it is set from outside the image. This post walks through a sample that uses the DLC exactly as published to fine-tune Qwen2.5-1.5B with PyTorch Fully Sharded Data Parallel (FSDP) across eight NVIDIA L4 GPUs on two g6.12xlarge instances. The training code is one function, the cluster is one RayCluster manifest plus a file of variables, and no image is built at any point. Because the DLC already carries the EFA stack, collectives between the two instances run over the EFA as soon as the pods request it. The entire solution is in this sample repository , and it uses the same KubeRay-on-EKS foundation as our multi-node Ray Serve walkthrough . What you get without building anything The Ray Train DLC is the PyTorch training image with Ray’s training libraries on top. title: Accelerating software delivery with agentic QA automation using Amazon Nova Act – Part 3
abstract: As quality assurance (QA) automation adoption grows inside an organization, a new problem appears that has nothing to do with writing tests. A platform team stands up test automation, then a second team wants to join, then a dozen more. Soon hundreds of test cases belong to different products and squads, and everyone can see everyone else’s tests. No one can answer a basic question at a glance: is this application’s test coverage healthy right now? Test authoring stops being the bottleneck. Organizing tests and controlling who can touch them becomes the work. A second, related question follows close behind: who owns this application and its tests, and who is accountable when coverage slips? Without a clear owner, health problems have no one to land on. In the first post , we introduced QA Studio, a reference solution built with Amazon Nova Act . Teams use it to define tests in natural language and run them through AI-powered visual navigation. In the second post , we added test suites and a CLI for batch regression testing in continuous integration and continuous delivery (CI/CD) pipelines. In this post, we cover two capabilities that help QA Studio scale across an organization. The first, applications , organizes tests and reports health metrics. The second, team-based user management , controls who can see and change what. Organizing tests with applications An application in QA Studio represents the system under test: a website, a web app, a service front end. It’s the container that gives a collection of tests, a home, and an owner. Use cases (the individual tests from Part 1) and test suites (the regression collections from Part 2) belong to an application, and they inherit its ownership. Instead of one flat list of every test in the deployment, each team works inside the applications they own. Creating an application takes a name, a base URL, and an optional set of environments such as development, staging, and production. From the application page, teams create new use cases directly in context, add existing ones, and group them into test suites. This is also where QA Studio reports on the health of the tests it runs. Figure 1: The application detail page, showing pass rate, executions, and failures with the use cases and test suites tabs Understanding application health with metrics Tests produce results. Understanding those results over time is what tells a team whether the development lifecycle for an application is healthy, not only whether a single build is ready for release. QA Studio records the outcome of every execution as Amazon CloudWatch custom metrics, dimensioned by application and by environment. It turns these metrics into a health view on the application page. The top of the page answers the immediate question with three figures: the pass rate over the selected window, the total number of executions, and the current failure count. Alongside them, QA Studio computes a health score of 0–100. The score starts from the pass rate and subtracts a penalty for flaky tests. That way, an application whose tests pass but flip between pass and fail doesn’t present a falsely perfect picture. A team scanning a portfolio of applications can tell the stable ones from the ones that need attention without opening each result. The metrics tab moves from the current snapshot to trends. Teams choose a 7-day window with hourly granularity or a 30-day window with daily granularity, and QA Studio charts executions, successes, failures, and average duration across that period. Because the underlying metrics carry an environment dimension, teams filter the view to a single environment. For example, they can compare how staging behaves against production for the same set of tests. Two views target the tests that cost teams the most time. abstract: This event summary was created by Claude with light editing by Tim O’Reilly, based on a transcript of the event. On October 15, 2026, Tim O’Reilly hosted Andrew Odewahn, CTO of O’Reilly Media, for an hour-long episode of Live with Tim O’Reilly , the interview series streamed live on the O’Reilly learning platform. Andrew has been at O’Reilly for many years, starting as an author, then building tools for the company’s platform, then eventually as CTO and head of engineering. Over the past year, his team has been building what the company calls Expert Intelligence , a suite of tools that connects an AI agent to an organization’s own systems, gives it a skill file describing how to reason about what it finds there, and grounds its analysis in the practitioner frameworks of the O’Reilly library. Andrew described the work in a recent Radar piece, “ Building Organizational Intelligence .” Tim and Andrew’s interview was organized around a presentation in two parts, the first on the research agent and the second on the system Andrew’s team built for reviewing what it produces, with discussion in between and audience questions throughout. Tim framed the conversation by asking a question he said Andrew’s work helps to answer: Most of the AI story is about efficiency, doing the same work faster. What does it look like for an organization to get smarter? Building the research agent Andrew’s research agent emerged from a personal need rather than a strategy. He wanted to know the status of a project, for example, how long a migration from RabbitMQ to Pub/Sub would take. This is the kind of question every engineer dreads but every engineering leader has to answer. He also had a broader concern. A single person being good at AI isn’t the same as an organization being good at it. He built his agent in four steps. He mapped the organization’s information systems as a hierarchy, connected them via MCP, wrote a skill telling the agent how to use them, and finally added the Expert Intelligence layer. The map of the sources of truth in the engineering organization’s workflows was what made the rest work. Andrew put them in order and explained to the model how they relate: Strategic goals and feature priorities live in Productboard. Those become epics, sprints, and stories in Jira. Stories become code in GitHub. A service catalog describes the roughly 300 services that make up the O’Reilly platform and who owns them, and observability tools show how those services perform against their SLOs. The skill also had to encode local quirks. Some teams mark an epic as finished with an end date, while others consider it done when every ticket is closed. Andrew also told the agent it was a research agent, not a coding agent, and that its job was to write reports. Connecting everything through MCP was, in his words, “the most completely tedious step of the whole process.” Productboard had no MCP server at the time, so he wrote a wrapper. Later, when Tim asked how another company could repeat the work with a different set of tools, Andrew suggested starting from the vendor list. Export it from your procurement system, ask the model what products those vendors make and which would hold information relevant to the questions you care about, and have it put them in order. O’Reilly product managers are now turning this process into a skill for the forthcoming Expert Intelligence Skills Hub. One audience member asked whether MCP was really the right tool for internal knowledge, compared with semantic search. As Andrew pointed out, sometimes anything is better than nothing. Ultimately, what you want is to give the model the ability to search across your systems. From a hiring case to a toil audit The center of the presentation was a before-and-after comparison of the particular use case that Andrew had previously written up in his “Building Organizational Intelligence” article. title: This Week in AI: Agents Rewrite the Rules
abstract: AI agents dominated the news this week, from security exploits that unfolded in hours to new tools that let agents shop, manage transactions, and conduct scientific research. On the latest episode of This Week in AI , host Vicki Reyzelman of Akamai examined how these developments are testing existing security practices and creating new opportunities for businesses and researchers. AI attacks are outpacing traditional security responses AI is changing how attackers find and exploit vulnerabilities. A supply chain attack involving ARTEX , an open source agentic AI penetration-testing framework, helped attackers reach more than 2,250 Microsoft 365 tenants through a ConnectWise compromise. The incident raised concerns about OAuth authentication and the limitations of conventional identity protections when autonomous agents interact with enterprise systems. A more immediate threat came from PHP2Shell , two vulnerabilities rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale that could allow attackers to execute code on vulnerable web servers without authentication. CISA urged immediate patching following the October 21 disclosure. Researchers also documented attackers using AI agents to obtain password hashes and MFA secrets from a European government system within two hours. The speed of exploitation leaves organizations little time to investigate threats before responding, especially smaller businesses with limited security resources. Security teams can no longer rely on manual review alone. They need automated detection and response, tighter access controls, and network segmentation to limit what compromised agents can reach. But monitoring autonomous agents is challenging. Researchers from METR and Redwood Research identified weaknesses in an earlier version of OpenAI’s internal monitoring system, including one that could allow hundreds of agent actions to be concealed. OpenAI says it has patched vulnerabilities affecting production safeguards, although the researchers haven’t independently evaluated those changes. The debate over AI safety is also extending beyond technical safeguards. Anthropic proposed federal AI safety legislation , while Google DeepMind employees resigned over the company’s military AI work. Both developments illustrate the growing pressure on AI companies to establish clearer rules for how their technology is developed and used. The transition to agents brings new challenges Retailers are taking different approaches to autonomous shopping. Walmart introduced an Agent Gateway that lets approved agents shop within customer-defined spending limits and approval requirements. Amazon has restricted some third-party shopping agents, while banks including Morgan Stanley and Bank of America are limiting agent access to customer accounts. The disagreement goes beyond security. Retailers that depend on advertising and product recommendations have an incentive to keep shoppers on their websites. As more purchases begin with agents, companies will have to reconsider how they maintain customer relationships. Anthropic is testing a different approach to agent oversight. Claude’s auto mode is becoming the default for Pro, Max, and Team users, allowing automated checks to approve routine actions and block risky ones. Anthropic also contributed its Agent Skills format to the Agentic AI Foundation under the Linux Foundation. More than 70 platforms have adopted the standard, with over a million skills published. Shared formats could make workflows easier to reuse across products, although organizations still need to control which actions those workflows can perform. Growing agent use also requires more computing capacity and electricity. We discussed NVIDIA’s $164.5 billion in commitments and guarantees supporting AI data centers, including an Ohio campus that SB Energy is building for OpenAI.
