title: Who Governs What an Agent Learns?
abstract: The following article originally appeared on Tim O’Brien’s Medium blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. I think we’re missing something in the conversation about agent security. We keep asking whether an agent has the right “identity” and “credentials.” Whether its credentials expire fast enough. Whether it can access a database or perform a particular task. Those questions matter. But they leave a much harder question underneath: Does the agent have permission to conceive of the situation in that way? As agents retain memories and acquire new skills, we need mechanisms that govern changes to the world model they can perceive and act on—and prevent those changes from silently expanding their authority. (Governing ontological change while preserving the boundaries of delegated authority.) An Interesting Morning by the Beach (AI assist from OpenAI) Agent security needs semantic and epistemic governance: Mechanisms that govern the model of the world an agent may act on, the evidence it may accept, and who may approve changes to either. An agent can learn without automatically gaining authority to act on everything it learns. These systems don’t need “awareness” to create this problem (and discussions of consciousness are unhelpful science fiction). They can retain information, revise procedures, and use what they have learned in subsequent work. That learning may happen through memory or updated skills while the underlying language model remains unchanged. We are responsible for governing what that learning allows them to do. Flatland gives me a way to explain why In Edwin Abbott’s novella , a Square lives in a two-dimensional world. A visiting Sphere introduces him to a third dimension. At first, the Square struggles to make sense of it. His familiar categories cannot explain what he is encountering. Eventually, his conception of the world changes. What interests me is the difference between simply acquiring another fact and changing the framework through which facts make sense. An agent’s ontology ( Gruber’s definition ) supplies an explicit framework of concepts and relationships. What counts as a customer? A contract? An emergency? How are those things connected? It is part of the model of the world we give the system to work with. And when an agent’s decisions depend on that framework, changing it can change the agent’s effective authority. We have already seen agents change what their environment means During the OpenAI evaluations associated with the Hugging Face incident, agents repurposed Artifactory, a system for storing and retrieving software packages, as a message board. They encoded messages in directory names, discovered other agents, shared information, and began assigning work to one another. METR reports that the main channel could be created with the minimal permissions needed to install packages ( read METR’s investigation ). A package cache became a “mailbox.” Other agent runs became “collaborators.” Messages became “assignments.” The popular story is that these agents “broke out” of a system, but they did what agents do well these days—they learned and adapted. This wasn’t so much about permissions as it was about an autonomous system adapting its operating model to achieve a result. (Thankfully no one asked it to make paperclips.) That is the operating-model change I’m concerned about. The agents discovered relationships and possibilities the intended environment hadn’t accounted for, then acted on them. The resulting collaboration helped coordinate attacks on Hugging Face infrastructure. ( Read OpenAI’s account .) We need mechanisms that distinguish discovering a possible use from being authorized to adopt it. Access to shared infrastructure must not automatically confer authority to establish a communications network or accept instructions from whoever appears there. But to be clear, these agents were doing exactly what they were asked to do. Who approved this? This is why givin

title: Cheap Code, Expensive Confidence
abstract: I recently used a coding agent to build Task Viewer, a small community helper for IBM Bob that we use internally at IBM. It’s a convenience plug-in to Bob, with no critical production role. Despite helping some users internally, for me it’s a real-world experiment on a project to find out how much of the implementation I can delegate. How much to delegate also depends on what the person doing the task still needs to learn. Someone familiar with the application may already know how to check the result, while a developer learning the system may need to work through part of the implementation to develop that understanding. Even when I hand all the coding to an agent, my basic requirements for myself are to check functionality and the design manually. I want to use the application and see whether it behaves the way I intended. Does the design make sense when I actually have to find something? Is the information presented in a way that I can follow? Those are questions I still need to spend time with, even when the application is small and the implementation was largely delegated. For Task Viewer, I also created plenty of UI tests to check that the data appeared correctly. That gave me a way to repeat some of the checks as the application changed. There was still a separate question about the calculations, though. Seeing a number in the right place on the screen does not tell me whether it’s the right number. I ran SQL queries against the underlying data to check the math, going back to the records the application was supposed to represent. There is quite a bit of understanding involved in that seemingly ordinary step. To check a calculation, you need to know what the result is supposed to mean and which records should contribute to it. You need some expectation against which to compare what the application displays. Thankfully, I had help from the team in uncovering relationships in the data that I would not have been able to derive or even explain on my own. For this particular application, I could inspect both its behavior and the data behind it, and I had people to turn to when my own understanding was incomplete. Its limited role also gave me room to experiment without making the result part of a production system. Building that confidence took time, because I had to check the behavior, establish what the numbers should mean, and resolve the questions I could not answer myself. All of that, for me, belongs in the assessment of how much coding I could delegate. This is why I find descriptions such as “The agent got me 80% of the way there” increasingly difficult to interpret. I understand the feeling behind them. You have something running, most of the interface exists, and it looks as though the remaining effort should be the smaller part. But a calculation based on the wrong records may look perfectly reasonable until you find a way to check it. Before correcting anything, you have to discover where your understanding and the application’s behavior diverge. The agent may help with that investigation too, although the amount of code it has already produced tells you very little about how long it will take. DORA’s analysis of 1,110 responses from Google software engineers describes some of the time saved during code generation being used for auditing and verification, alongside productivity benefits. I would expect to check an application I had implemented myself too, so any comparison needs to include the time it takes to reach a result we are prepared to use. Otherwise, we can make agentic development look unusually expensive by counting checks we leave out of the human version, or unusually cheap by stopping the clock when the agent says it has finished. Some of that effort can make later changes easier to accept. Once a UI test exercises an important behavior, it can keep doing so as the application changes, and a calculation checked against a small set of records can become a regression test. title: The PHP Incident
abstract: The PHP security incident is now (almost) old news. The timeline looks something like this : In late August, Wiz Research discovered two serious remote code execution vulnerabilities in PHP called PHP2Shell. They reported the vulnerabilities to the PHP team on August 24, which started working on fixes on September 21. Amazon apparently detected PHP2Shell in the wild on October 17 (four days prior to disclosure). On October 20, details of the two vulnerabilities (CVE-2026-109618 and CVE-2026-109619) were leaked prematurely. The next day, October 21, the PHP team released patches. If that were the end of the story, it wouldn’t be notable. But the problem goes a lot deeper. Although PHP is no longer fashionable, it runs a huge portion of the public internet. WordPress, Drupal, and Wikimedia run on top of PHP, and people who build on top of these tools are understandably not interested in chasing the latest hot technology. “ Choose Boring Technology ” is one of my favorite technical essays, and PHP is nothing if not boring. It’s well known and understood, and replacing something so widely used subjects you to a steep learning curve and new bugs and vulnerabilities. One problem is that PHP has a long history. According to Wiz, the vulnerabilities are present in versions going back to PHP 5.4. The PHP Foundation has released PHP 8.5.12, 8.4.27, 8.3.36, and 8.2.35, and said that all instances of PHP need to be updated to one of those releases. Sites that can’t be updated should be taken offline and isolated. Upgrading an ancient PHP installation is a task that’s likely to fall on organizations least capable of undertaking it. There are plenty of ancient WordPress installations that haven’t been updated in years. There were so many fires to put out, and PHP pretty much “just worked”; running an old version wasn’t causing problems, and with so much else to do, why ask for trouble? Unfortunately, choosing boring technology doesn’t mean ignoring updates. And those who decided not to ask for trouble are now in plenty of trouble. This situation demonstrates the power of the latest foundation models to uncover vulnerabilities. Wiz used Wiz Atlas (its own model), Gemini 4 Argon, and GPT-5.6 Sol to discover the vulnerability, which isn’t a single bug but a combination of several bugs that have been present for years but were obscure enough and apparently harmless enough to escape detection or repair. As Wiz says, The underlying flaws had been present for decades, but demonstrating their exploitability required an exceptionally complex chain of steps, at the edge of what human researchers could practically achieve. Frontier AI models substantially reduced that barrier, turning a longstanding flaw into an exploit. That’s the new frontier in security: finding ways to exploit chains of minor, unfixed, and sometimes undiscovered bugs in novel ways. Wiz was working responsibly with the PHP team to repair the vulnerability. The implications of this, however, are far broader than the fix to PHP, or even the thousands of PHP sites that need upgrades and are now vulnerable to attack. This incident shows dramatically how the gap between the discovery of a vulnerability and its exploitation has dropped. Since exploitation began before the RCEs were prematurely leaked, it makes sense to assume that some other organization had access to models capable of discovering the vulnerability. Gemini 4 Argon and GPT-5.6 Sol are publicly available, though with guardrails that limit their usefulness for security research. I’m willing to assume that Wiz had access to the unrestricted version, but I doubt that the PHP team did. There are certainly other models, including open-weight models, that could be used to find vulnerabilities. Regardless of your stance on restricting model capabilities (I think those limitations are more damaging than helpful), it’s clear that Pandora’s box has been opened. title: Are You Getting Your Money’s Worth From AI?
abstract: The following article was originally published on James Shore’s Successful Software blog and is being republished here with the author’s permission. Software development has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of AI automation. One CIO I talked to recently, with 170 people in his organization, measured a 2.1x increase in productivity from AI. That productivity came at a cost. His top users of AI each spent $21,000 on tokens per month. Another engineering leader spends six to eight thousand dollars per engineer per month. This is not a trivial amount of money. Eventually, it has to come from somewhere, and it will probably come from your personnel budget. Now we’re talking about real consequences for real people’s lives. But there are also real business consequences for not acting. If you’re going to make those choices—and somebody is going to—they need to be good ones. So you need to know more than the costs; you need to know the benefits too. Are you getting a good return on your investment in AI? Is there another way of using AI that would be better? How do you know what you’re getting? Anecdotal reports abound, but the reasoning behind those anecdotes are often, to put it politely, not ideal. Some claims are outright fiction. Given the stakes, that’s a problem. In this essay series, I’ll show you how to assess the impact of AI on software development in your organization. It’s in four parts plus an epilogue: Why, and what not to do (this essay) Measuring delivery speed Measuring and modeling unintended consequences Modeling and forecasting business outcomes Epilogue: Notes for your CFO Why you need to quantify impact Engineering leaders everywhere are feeling pressure to do more with AI. But which approach is best? There are a lot of people with strident opinions about what to do, but not a lot of consensus, and even less hard data. Even if there were hard data, it’s not one-size-fits-all. A solution that works best for an internal IT development shop isn’t necessarily the one that works best for a startup, and the approach that’s best for a new product isn’t necessarily the one that’s best for a crafty legacy system. Faster approaches aren’t necessarily better, either. If you get twice as much done per person, but spend so much money on tokens that you have to cut your staff in half, have you actually seen any ROI? You might actually be better off with a more modest speed boost if it keeps your costs down. You can’t make these trade-offs from a gut feeling alone. In a famous METR study , engineers thought AI made them 49% faster than it actually did. 1 You have to measure impact to know what you’re actually getting. Don’t neglect costs Costs are much easier to measure than impact, but they’re not without their own challenges. The biggest one is subsidies. In the fight to gain market share, big AI firms are offering substantial discounts. One engineering leader told me each team member was spending thousands of dollars in tokens at the cost of a $200 subscription. Anthropic and OpenAI are constantly offering discounts and other promotions. At some point, these subsidies will end, and prices will go up. Or will they? Open-weight models and local inference are exerting downward pressure on token costs. Dedicated inference chips could make tokens cheaper. Routers promise to direct your prompts to the cheapest model for the job. Models could require fewer tokens to accomplish the same task as they become more capable. All of these factors could actually cause prices to go down. When you calculate ROI, don’t assume today’s costs are the ones you should model. Whether you think prices will go up, down, or remain the same, make your assumptions explicit, and consider modeling both optimistic and pessimistic scenarios. One more wrinkle: Adopting AI isn’t a matter of flipping a switch. People will need time to learn how to apply it. As with any big shift, change management isn’t to be underestimated. Here’s how they could make an already growing problem worse . —Jessica Hamzelou This story is from The Checkup, our weekly biotech newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Thursday. title: Eating disorders are on the rise. GLP-1s could make things worse.
abstract: GLP-1 weight-loss drugs are one of the biggest biotech breakthroughs of the last decade. But to some clinical psychologists, they can represent something more sinister—a potential trigger for eating disorders. A new report suggests that the global incidence of anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa shot up between 1990 and 2023—by a whopping 71%. By 2023, there were an estimated 18.1 million people living with one of these two disorders. What’s worse is that the number is likely to be much higher than that once we factor in other eating disorders. And, disturbingly, those in the field are already starting to see GLP-1 weight-loss drugs exacerbating the issue. Cheri Levinson is a clinical psychologist at the University of Louisville in Kentucky who has specialized in eating disorders for almost 20 years. She says she’s now seeing more patients with more severe symptoms than at any other time in her career, and that many of them are misusing GLP-1s. “This is the worst I’ve seen things,” she says. Eating disorders are mental health conditions in which people’s eating behaviors impact their health. They include anorexia nervosa (defined by a fear of weight gain), bulimia nervosa (in which people binge and purge), binge eating disorder, and others. It’s thought that some people have a genetic predisposition to certain eating disorders, but that some external factor is what triggers their onset. That might be stress, or social pressure to be skinny. Often, simply restricting food intake can trigger an eating disorder, says Levinson. Eating disorders—along with the pressure to look thin—were already prevalent in the 1990s (the heroin chic era springs to mind). To find out how things might have changed since then, Ruhai Bai at the Children’s Hospital of Nanjing Medical University in China and his colleagues pulled together data from studies and surveys conducted on populations around the world. The team used statistical models to fill in any data gaps. That research allowed the researchers to estimate the annual incidence of two eating disorders—anorexia nervosa and bulimia nervosa—for each of 204 countries and territories between 1990 and 2023. They also estimated the impact those disorders had on global health by calculating their disability-adjusted life years (one DALY represents a year of healthy life lost). The findings, published in JAMA Psychiatry on Wednesday, are unsettling. Between 1990 and 2023, there was a 71% increase in the incidence of those two eating disorders, the team found. Those conditions had a huge impact on global health, too. In 2023, they “cost the world the equivalent of about 3.83 million years of healthy life,” says Bai. Bai and his colleagues expect these figures to continue to rise. In 2023, an estimated 18.1 million people had either anorexia nervosa or bulimia nervosa; by 2050, the team predict, the two conditions could affect 21.8 million people. It gets worse. Those two conditions represent less than half of all eating disorders, says Levinson, who was not involved in Bai’s study. The true impact of these disorders is “probably three times the rate that they’re reporting,” she says. Bai and his colleagues didn’t explore the reasons for this rise (although Bai points out that it can’t be entirely explained by population growth). So how did we get here? Social media may have played a role. “Social media comparisons, influencers, challenges, diet trends can all be precipitating … events for an eating disorder,” says Cynthia Bulik, a clinical psychologist at the University of North Carolina, who was not involved in the new study. Bulik has been studying and treating eating disorders since the early 1980s. “Between 1990 and 2023 there has clearly been an upsurge of those types of environmental exposures,” she says. title: We urgently need to monitor AI agents’ actions in real time
abstract: This summer, hundreds of OpenAI agents tried to cheat on a cybersecurity test. They broke out of their test environment and successfully hacked Hugging Face, a site that they believed held clues about how they’d be graded. Around the same time, another OpenAI agent accessed private files from an Australian government website. It’s a problem that’s by no means confined to OpenAI. In the months since, Anthropic, Google, and Meta have also disclosed incidents in which their agents have gone off track. And worryingly, in many cases the agents eluded the very researchers and safety teams tasked with monitoring them. AI agents are taking unauthorized actions, and the companies building and running them are mostly relying on luck and hindsight to mitigate any harmful impacts. They must do more to ensure safety. That’s why EU regulators and US agencies are rightfully calling for agent developers and deployers to monitor agents in real time. But these rules assume that companies can see what their agents are doing and why—when in reality, they lack sufficient visibility. Imagine a bank hiring a thousand new employees who can access customer accounts and sensitive information, but the employees’ ID badges change every day, it’s not clear whether a manager ever reviewed or authorized their work, and nobody logs the changes employees make to approval processes. That lack of visibility is where we are with agents today. As agents roll out across critical sectors, from finance to government to medicine , we must be able to monitor them in real time to prevent wide-ranging and potentially devastating consequences. And while safety depends on monitoring, monitoring requires observability : the capacity to capture what the system did, process it into signals, and present those to humans or automated oversight systems. In other words, we need to know what the agent did and why it did it. And as our recent research shows, current agent frameworks—the software that runs agents— do not reliably generate the crucial observability records we need to ensure that agents are deployed safely. Agents present new kinds of problems that generative AI alone does not. They inherit the unpredictability of the LLMs they are built on, but where a generative AI system produces a single output for a human to act on, an agent performs longer tasks—it plans, picks tools, spawns sub-agents, and takes actions. So an agent’s course can take shape in a multitude of different ways, and no tests before launch can fully anticipate the risks. This makes observing the agents while they work even more challenging, and even more important. With colleagues from academia, civil society, and industry, we studied the four most widely used agent frameworks to see what signals they actually emit. We found major gaps that made it hard to achieve key safety goals, like noticing policy violations, unauthorized actions, and even human oversight failures. Key observability requirements were missing—like Agent IDs that persist over time, and records about which humans approved agent tasks. This made it hard to tell which agents did what or assess whether they were taking unauthorized actions. The good news is that these gaps, once identified, can be closed. Doing so starts with capturing two types of records: those that reveal what happened in an agent’s run and how the agent made its decisions. The “what happened” records identify the agent (while preserving privacy) and log how humans intervened and whether agent permissions or “memory” shifted, while the “decision” records show an agent’s reasoning and levels of confidence in the actions it’s taken. Take, for example, agents working to process a bank’s mortgage loans. The system examines an application and recommends denying it, and then a human loan officer signs off on the decision. In a later audit, or perhaps even in real time, a bank or regulator needs to be able to reconstruct which agent made the call, which officer approved it

title: Our climate models have a big, dangerous blind spot
abstract: Climate change itself is increasingly fueling climate change. Rising concentrations of greenhouse gases are driving up global temperatures, setting off dangerous feedback loops that we have not fully accounted for in our climate models—or our emissions-reduction goals. Scientists have long warned that warming would propel further warming in various ways, but a growing number of observations and studies are at last providing a sharper sense of just how powerful these cascading effects could be. And, by extension, they’re showing how much faster the planet may warm in this century. A study in Environmental Research Letters in September, synthesizing the results of previous papers, found that the additional carbon dioxide and methane released from thawing permafrost, intensifying wildfires, hotter lakes and reservoirs , and wetter, warmer wetlands alone could drive global average temperatures up 0.2 °C to 0.4 °C this century. That would come on top of the 2.6°C of warming above preindustrial levels that modelers are already expecting through 2100. The additional heat could subject many of the world’s cities to monthslong heat waves and expose hundreds of millions of people to flooding. None of the models that inform the major UN climate reports, which assess how much the planet will likely warm under various emissions scenarios, account for all these feedback effects. Many of them don’t incorporate any. That leaves a huge blind spot in our understanding of how much the world could actually warm in the coming decades—and how rapidly nations will need to slash emissions to stay within critical boundaries. A separate analysis published in One Earth in March , which examined what the feedback problem means for our international climate goals, concluded that the world may be much further off track than is widely believed. It found that just three regional sources of warming-driven emissions—thawing permafrost, increasing fires in boreal forests, and warming tropical wetlands—may shorten by as much as 25% the time before the planet consistently breaches the 1.5 °C and 2 °C warming thresholds. Our climate models and the UN’s reports clearly need to be updated to better represent these effects. Nations must also step up their efforts to reduce emissions to reflect this improving understanding of the dangers we face, says Sam Abernethy, the lead author of the paper and a climate scientist at Spark Climate Solutions, a San Francisco–based nonprofit research group. At least some of this is starting to happen. Spark kick-started an initiative, called the Warming-Induced Greenhouse Gas Emissions Model Intercomparison Project , through which more than 20 international teams are running the same set of analyses on different models to develop greater understanding of feedback effects’ potential power. Researchers involved hope that the UN will incorporate those results into its next major climate assessment, due out in 2029. That report will update estimates of the remaining emissions that can be released before the world crosses key temperature thresholds. But what is already clear is that the planet is rapidly warming and that nations haven’t done nearly enough to cut fossil-fuel pollution. And even if we did manage to halt it, warming-driven emissions could continue. So a number of the research groups involved in the recent studies have started to explore what nations could do to get feedback emissions under control. Scientists at the Woodwell Climate Research Center in Massachusetts are, for example, investigating the possibility of preventing fires or rapidly detecting them and putting them out when they threaten to burn the vegetation and soil that help insulate particularly carbon-rich wedges of permafrost (a subject I explored at length in a recent feature story ). title: Creating AI value with enterprise context
abstract: Across a business, any number of AI platforms, systems, and tools may be at work simultaneously—for example, AI-powered customer platforms, conversational assistants, and workflow and process automation tools. Each one is sophisticated, advanced, and quick to respond. But, when set to work, the outcomes and actions that emerge may be wrong, confused, or lacking a proper understanding of the business. Many organizations find themselves in this situation—and it could be one of key reasons they struggle to extract returns on their AI investments. DOWNLOAD THE REPORT An MIT Technology Review Insights poll finds that while every organization surveyed is using AI today to some degree, fewer than one in five (16%) are extracting transformative value from their deployments. The largest percentage of respondents (40%) say they are seeing moderate gains in specific tasks or teams, while 21% report meaningful gains, leaving 23% that are seeing minimal returns or none at all. Companies are mostly still piloting AI use cases (according to 38% of respondents) or using it to assist employees’ work with tools like co-pilots or chat assistants (35%). Just 12% of enterprises have AI agents in production and 3% say they are using AI to do most of the work in key processes. “There’s a big gap between what the models are capable of and how the models are actually being useful inside organizations,” says Prukalpa Sankar, co-founder of Atlan. “For every real-life intent and purpose, artificial general intelligence is already here. It’s just not really useful in most companies today.” The missing layer, Sankar says, is context, or how well AI understands a business. A context layer is the architectural infrastructure that sits between an organization’s business systems (for example, systems of record and data, and its AI platforms). It translates enterprise intelligence into governed, machine-usable context for AI agents or models and helps knowledge compound. “Without a context layer for AI, it’s almost like you’re hiring the smartest intern in the world, blindfolding them, and throwing them into your organization,” Sankar says. Download the report This content was produced by Insights, MIT Technology Review’s custom content arm, not its editorial staff. It was researched and written by humans, with any AI tools that may have been used limited to production processes under human oversight.

title: The Download: dead startups fueling AI and interspecies communication
abstract: This is today’s edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. AI labs are buying data from dead startups to train their models When Keelan Miskell began winding down his crypto startup, he didn’t think its data was worth much. But he’s since turned the company’s digital archives into tens of thousands of dollars, selling its codebase and workspace data. He’s part of a growing market in which companies that help shut down startups sell their data to AI labs. Demand has grown as training labs hit the limits of public and synthetic datasets, with buyers seeking real-world records to help train AI agents. But the sales raise legal and ethical questions. Read the full story on the AI labs buying up the remains of failed startups . —Matthew King Are we there yet? Interspecies communication Humans are far from the only species with a gift for gab, and our furry, feathered, and finned friends could have a lot to tell us. Decoding how animals communicate with one another could reveal the inner lives of other species—and give humans a window onto how they see the world. A growing arsenal of devices and advances in AI have made it easier to study their howls, squeaks, and clicks, but making sense of it all remains complex. Find out how close we are to interspecies communication . —Cassandra Willyard This story is part of “Are we there yet?” , our series that takes stock of six technologies that have long promised to change the world—and scores them on a progress meter. We’re exploring each one in The Download, so stay tuned, and subscribe to read the rest of the stories in our new Impossible issue . MIT Technology Review Narrated: what it would take to build a city on the moon The US and China are racing to build bases on the moon, with NASA hoping to establish a small lunar city by the end of the century. But the moon is a tremendously hostile place to set up camp. A sprawling lunar base must be safe for its inhabitants, protected from falling asteroids, endless cosmic radiation, razor-sharp lunar dust, and torturous temperature swings. It also must be somewhat self-sustaining. That will require autonomous robots, nuclear power, and a way to use the moon’s resources to keep the base operating. But the chief obstacle may be one of political will . This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . title: Pairing industrial AI autonomy and human control
Consumer Appetite for Personal AI Goes Mainstream
abstract: This article is brought to you by Qualcomm Technologies . For many consumers, much of the promise and appeal of AI is personal. Consumers are looking past generic tools and want to know how these technologies will help them in their daily lives. These trends coincide with the advent of new classes of wearable devices that, in addition to being able to leverage powerful frontier models, feature built-in intelligence that understand the context of a user. Where are they? What are they seeing and hearing? What are their habits, their preferences, their schedules? It’s an astonishing pivot, from passive accessories that served mostly to send users smartphone notifications to proactive, intelligent companions. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. And it shifts the focus toward you, the user. These new technologies are exciting. But what do consumers really want? A Personal AI report , commissioned by Qualcomm Technologies, built on a survey of more than 12,000 people across key geographies worldwide (the U.S., U.K., Germany, India, Brazil, and China) focused on the rise of personal AI in intelligent wearables looks deeply at these developments. The smartphone is no longer the center of that universe; though it’s still incredibly important, in this personal AI paradigm, the AI is the UI. Survey respondents are less interested in single devices and are responding more to the idea of connected ecosystems. As people expand their roster of devices, it only makes sense. Instead of relying entirely on a smartphone and a laptop, respondents also have connected technology in their cars, as well as intelligent wearables like smartwatches, smart glasses, hearables, and other wearables like rings, pins, and pendants. They want those devices to work in concert, and the way to do that is to decentralize any single one of them. Instead, the AI agent that knows the user and works across all of those devices becomes the unifying factor. Consider a typical workday: A user’s watch detects it is time to leave for a meeting and, with permission, their AI agent factors in calendar details, real-time traffic and battery status across their devices. In the car, it suggests the best route and briefs them on their meeting agenda. As they arrive, smart glasses surface a discreet reminder, such as the meeting location or the name of a new contact, while the phone stays in their pocket. No one device has to do everything; each plays the role it is best suited for, coordinated by a personal AI agent that understands the user’s context and acts only at the user’s direction. With this in mind, simply adding more hardware to the mix isn’t sufficient. Even though respondents will be open to new form factors, they’ll demand more from their ecosystem of devices. They’ll be sensitive to points of friction and needless complexity, and they’ll require each new device to bring something new to the table — “incremental intelligence, convenience, or contextual awareness that their existing devices cannot deliver on their own what the report,” reads the report. The usage trends are up. The report found that those who own wearables are already using AI frequently (60 percent use it at least weekly), which indicates that it’s becoming less of a fun experiment for early adopters and more of a critical mass habit. The “always-on” nature of intelligent wearables appears to be winning respondents, too. The report found the following statistics on average continuous wear among users: True wireless earbuds – 3 hours Wireless headphones – 3 hours Smart glasses – 5 hours Audio glasses – 6 hours Smartwatches – 9 hours Smart rings, necklaces and pendants – 8 hours Consumers want AI that is personal and understands their context — they’re looking for smooth, intuitive experiences that are marked by privacy, security, and user control. title: Systems Thinking Is Vital in the Age of AI
abstract: Modern engineering projects increasingly combine human judgment with machine capability. An engineer can define a problem, then ask an artificial intelligence tool to search relevant research and technical standards, generate design options, test them in simulation, and compare the results. The engineer can then bring the results to specialists who understand the parts AI cannot judge on its own, such as whether a design can be built safely, whether it makes sense in a particular setting, or how it might affect its users. The final decision about whether and how to move forward remains a human responsibility. AI can help engineers do early project steps that once required several people with different technical skills. The engineer’s role is therefore expanding from performing each technical step to deciding how people, machines, and specialists’ knowledge should work together on the project. The problem, not the title Engineering has always been divided into disciplines, and for good reasons. Electrical, mechanical, civil, software, and other engineering fields require deep knowledge that takes years to develop. AI does not replace that need. It simply changes how easily engineers can explore the parts of a problem that sit outside their own specialty. Consider a software engineer working on a medical device . AI can help the engineer review relevant biomedical research, understand unfamiliar terms, analyze data, and build an early model. That does not make the engineer a physician or biomedical expert. It allows the engineer to ask better questions before working with the experts. The same is true in energy , transportation, manufacturing, and many other fields. A problem might begin as a software issue and then quickly involve hardware, safety measures, economics, human behavior, and regulations. Engineers do not need to master every field; they need to recognize which expertise the problem requires and bring the right people and tools together. The importance of systems thinking Systems thinking thus becomes especially important. It requires looking at the whole problem: understanding how its parts affect one another, identifying constraints and failure points, and making trade-offs. AI adds a new element to the process. Engineers must decide not only how the technical parts fit together but also what work to give to AI, what a person must check, when a specialist should make a decision, and when the problem needs to be redefined. An engineer’s value is not in knowing everything. It is in knowing how to frame the problem, how to ask the right questions, how to test the answers, and when another expert must lead the project. This aspect is crucial because technical challenges in engineering are seldom static. As new insights emerge, objectives might shift, unseen limitations can surface, and the initial premise might prove flawed. Rather than rigidly following the starting specifications, an effective engineer adapts and refines the scope as a deeper understanding of the system develops. Thus, engineering extends beyond mastering technical concepts; it is an adaptable, structured approach to navigating evolving challenges. New evidence can change the goal, reveal a hidden constraint, or show that the original hypothesis was wrong. Effective engineers go beyond merely acting on the initial problem statement. They update it as the system becomes better understood. In that sense, engineering is not only a body of technical knowledge, it is also a disciplined way of thinking about a project. Human judgment is important AI can produce convincing answers even when its assumptions are weak. It can generate code that works in one test but fails in another. It can summarize research without understanding which evidence is strongest, or optimize a design for the wrong goal. Such limits make human expertise more important, not less. Machines are useful where speed, scale, search, pattern recognition, and data generation matter. People

title: Think you can save the Hubble Space Telescope? NASA wants to know.
abstract: The Hubble Space Telescope still shines in the eyes of astronomers after 36 years in orbit, but it is not as nimble as it once was. Left alone, the observatory will plunge back into the atmosphere in the early-to-mid-2030s, closing the book on one of the most famous scientific instruments of the century. NASA last raised the orbit of Hubble in 2002, when the Space Shuttle Columbia visited the observatory for a servicing mission. The final shuttle servicing flight in 2009 did not reboost the telescope's orbit, and with the retirement of the shuttle fleet two years later, Hubble has steadily lost altitude with no way to stave off eventual destruction. The space agency released a Request For Information (RFI) on Thursday asking commercial companies for ideas on how to reboost, service, or a controlled disposal of Hubble. Responses are due November 30. Specifically, NASA is looking for information about companies' current and near-term capabilities for capturing Hubble and boosting it to an altitude of at least 373 miles (600 km), enhancing the telescope's performance through, or guiding Hubble to a controlled reentry. title: Flesh-eating screwworms spread to third state and are attacking pets
abstract: For a genuine fright this Halloween, you can turn your gaze to the southern border, where ravenous, flesh-eating maggots are festering and have taken to eating people's pets. This week, the country's New World Screwworm (NWS) infestation spread to a third state, Arizona, which joins New Mexico and Texas in being plagued by the horrifying parasites. To date, 74 animal cases have been identified in the US since the flies re-invaded the country in June. The flies lay hundreds of eggs in wounds and moist orifices of animals, and the resulting voracious maggots feast on their victims. The maggots resemble screws and tortuously bore and twist into living flesh, causing severe, sometimes fatal wounds, before dropping to the ground to develop into adults. Read full article Comments

title: Oh captain, our captain: Ars staff remembers Patrick Stewart
abstract: Along with the rest of the world, we at Ars are mourning Sir Patrick Stewart —the beloved award-winning actor best known as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation and Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men franchise—who died yesterday at the age of 86. A statement released by Stewart's representatives said: We announce with great sorrow the passing of Sir Patrick Stewart yesterday at his home in Los Angeles, in the loving care of his beloved wife Sunny, following a brief and poignant journey with Alzheimer’s Disease and Lewy Body Dementia. He has been held in the warm embrace of family and friends, surrounded by live music, prayer, tears, laughter, and the kind of profound emotion that only he could inspire after a lifetime of devotion to us all. We will forever cherish the peaceful ease and reflection on his face, an enduring reminder of his invincible grace. Through the actor's X account , the family has requested that, in lieu of flowers, memorial contributions be made to the Johns Hopkins Alzheimer’s Disease Research Center Fund and the Alzheimer’s Foundation of America Caregiver Resources . title: Supersonic airliner in doubt as company shifts to powering AI data centers
abstract: Boom Supersonic CEO Blake Scholl recently declared “it’s time for a renaissance in energy and in supersonic flight” as the supersonic airliner company unveiled a Colorado factory dedicated to making gas turbines for AI data centers. But Boom may be facing turbulence after early backers for both ventures have questioned the company’s delivery timeline or backed out entirely. One of the company’s first customers, United Airlines CEO Scott Kirby, has expressed doubts about Boom’s original plan to deliver the first Overture supersonic airliner in 2029. Kirby’s latest frank assessment came during an interview with the Office Hours: Business Edition podcast that appeared on October 28, 2026. “‘29 is their official timeline,” Kirby told podcast host Monica Langley. “It’s not going to happen in ‘29—it’s going to take longer.” Read full article Comments

title: Anthropic VS code extension on Cursor backdoored for nearly 12 hours
abstract: An official extension for Anthropic’s Claude model was backdoored and threatened as many as 5,000 developers' machines, multiple sources reported Friday. Anthropic so far has yet to warn customers of the incident. The compromised package was a VS Code extension available in the marketplace of Cursor, a maker of AI-assisted developer tools, the company said Friday. The malicious version, 2.1.313, subsequently affected “at most 5,000 users,” presumably when they either downloaded it or their systems automatically fetched and installed it. Anthropic pushed version 2.1.314 several hours after the previous version became available on Cursor, according to independent researcher Kevin Beaumont. Both Beaumont and the CTO and co-founder of security firm Phorian said that version 2.1.313 was distributed through Anthropic’s official account on Cursor. So far, neither Cursor nor Anthropic has explained how the attackers gained control of the account. In search of cloud credentials “It was a supply-chain compromise where the attacker gained access to the official distribution channel,” Phorian CTO and co-founder Luke Roberts told Ars. “The malicious version 2.1.313 was posted to the official Anthropic account, effectively superseding 2.1.312. Extensions auto-update in Cursor by default, but users can configure this in settings.” Phorian has more details here . Read full article Comments

title: Dartmouth's provost warned us about AI cheating—but his own AI use cost him his job
abstract: On August 9, 2026, Dartmouth College provost Santiago Schnell wrote a Washington Post op-ed called "Universities are fighting AI cheating. But there’s a deeper problem." This week, Schnell discovered the depths of the problem himself as he resigned from the university after an advisory committee found that he failed to disclose significant AI use in an academic paper and in the Washington Post op-ed, even though publishers required such disclosure. Schnell didn't make it especially easy for the committee to investigate his AI use; the report uses the term "insufficient cooperation." He did turn over his Dartmouth laptop, but he did not turn over logs from his personal LLM accounts related to the writings in question. Nor did he agree to meet with the committee. The committee did get access to the Claude enterprise account Schnell had used through Dartmouth, though. This shows him using the LLM as a tool for revising his papers, finding and fixing bugs in code, and editing or generating figures. title: Over 25% of people lie to get antibiotics—and their lies aren't even good
abstract: A significant number of patients in the US lie to their doctors to get antibiotics they likely don't need, according to two new studies. While that may not be a startling revelation, the studies drills down on the phenomenon, finding that the lies patients tell are generally bad ones—and yet, they work almost all the time. In the two linked studies published Friday in JAMA Network Open, a team of researchers led by Alistair Thorpe at the University of Utah analyzed online survey data from over 1,000 adults. They found that over a quarter of people reported having lied to a clinician at least once to get an antibiotic prescription for themselves or a child in their care. Patients lied by either exaggerating symptoms, making up symptoms, or—most often—both. But interestingly, the lies people told to get antibiotics involved making up or exaggerating symptoms of infections that wouldn't be treated with antibiotics. For example, the most common falsehoods were symptoms associated with colds, such as fever, cough, and sore throat. That's despite the fact that colds are caused by viruses, not bacteria—which antibiotics treat. Read full article Comments

title: Basically no one is using AI agents for their DoorDash orders
abstract: As AI tools and agents have continued their march across all aspects of digital life, many companies are trying to use LLMs to improve the experience of purchasing goods and services on the Internet. Thus far, though, a vanishingly small number of people seem to be taking advantage of those capabilities, at least when it comes to using the popular food delivery app DoorDash with an outside AI agent. In a third-quarter earnings call Thursday , DoorDash co-founder and CEO Tony Xu responded to an analyst question by noting that "AI agents are generating several hundred orders [on DoorDash] across the time that they've been up and running." In a marked understatement, Xu called this a "very low use case" for a company that handled just shy of 1 billion orders total in the third quarter of 2026 alone. Speaking generally, Xu said he sees the potential for AI agents to be genuinely helpful for "long consideration purchases" and major decisions where agents would be "doing work on your behalf proactively in the background." However, Xu added, "when it comes to a task that's as simple as ordering food, we tend to see that come directly to DoorDash." Read full article Comments

title: Rare meteorite from Mars gives us a view into its ancient crust
abstract: Crater counts tell us that most of the Martian surface is more than 3 billion years old, but pieces of Mars we have on Earth tell a different story. The three main classes of Martian meteorites—shergottites, nakhlites, and chassignites—are all 2.4 billion years old or younger. Until now, only two genuinely ancient Martian meteorites were known: Allan Hills 84001, found in Antarctica, and a jumbled rock from northwest Africa nicknamed Black Beauty. Now we have a third one. A team led by Yang Liu, a planetary scientist at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory, has shown that a Martian meteorite called Teghaza 001, found in the Sahara Desert in Mali in 2022, formed at least 4.1 billion years ago. “It's very old and similar to some of the oldest rocks on Earth,” Liu says. A filtered collection “We don't fully understand why old Martian rocks are so rare on Earth," Liu said. Part of the answer may lie in how a piece of Mars gets here. It takes a large impact to launch a rock off the planet, and not every rock can survive that. “If the impact hits into loose powder, it may not get cemented to become a rock and fly off Mars' gravity,” Liu said. “So the natural impact already acts as a filter. Weak rocks do not make it off Mars.” Read full article Comments

title: Fujifilm to boost tape production 5x as AI fuels archiving demand
abstract: In an announcement released Thursday, Fujifilm said it will invest roughly 10 billion yen (about $63 million) to increase its production capacity fivefold for an unlikely beneficiary of the AI era: magnetic tape. Fujifilm attributes the surge in archiving demand to the spread of generative AI, which the company remarked is producing "exponential growth" in data needs worldwide. The 5x increase in production capacity will be measured against fiscal year 2025 production levels. The investment in Fujifilm's Kanagawa Factory, Odawara site will make it "the largest investment Fujifilm has made to date in dedicated LTO tape facilities." The project will run from fiscal years 2026 through 2028 to fund manufacturing expansion and additional personnel, primarily to produce the latest-generation "FUJIFILM LTO Ultrium10" tape. title: Thousands of “ghost students” use AI to steal millions in student loans, DOJ says
abstract: The US has charged five individuals as part of the first broad federal crackdown on “ghost students”—fraudsters who steal the identities of hundreds of Americans to pose as fake college students and steal student loans. In a press release Thursday, the Department of Justice said it had uncovered a large-scale scheme relying partly on AI. The DOJ seized more than $750,000 in cryptocurrency from “a network associated with Kenyan nationals" after data analysis helped flag likely fraudsters. Assistant Attorney General Colin M. McDonald of the DOJ’s National Fraud Enforcement Division credited new fraud-detection measures implemented by the Trump administration for the arrests. He said that “this is the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya,” while warning fraudsters that the crackdown has only just begun. “If you steal American identities, if you steal taxpayer dollars, if you exploit programs meant to help students build a future—we will find you,” McDonald said. “Whether you are in Nebraska, New Jersey, Virginia, or Nairobi, we will pursue you.” Read full article Comments

title: Analysts find looming launch crisis is "more severe" than anticipated
abstract: A new report from the analytics firm Quilty Space confirms that, outside of China, the world faces a significant shortage of rockets over the next five years. The firm estimates that between now and 2030, there will be a shortfall of about 150 launches compared to demand from satellite operators and civil space agencies. If demand from the US military is added in—and SpaceX does not extend the Falcon 9 and Falcon Heavy program to accommodate increased national security needs—the shortage could be doubled. "What we wanted to get at is to understand how severe this launch crisis is and when will it be resolved," said Caleb Henry, director of research at Quilty Space. "What we learned is that the launch crisis is more severe than we thought and that it will not go away this decade for sure, and it might not abate until sometime late in the 2030s." title: GM to pay $220 million after selling customer Smart Driver data
abstract: General Motors marketed its Smart Driver system as a way for parents to monitor teen drivers or for adults to track their driving behavior. But in 2024, it emerged that GM had been sharing that data with brokers. Those brokers then sold the data to insurance companies , and some drivers found that their insurance became more expensive as a result. To make matters worse, many of those drivers claimed they had no knowledge of ever agreeing to share such data for such purposes. Last year , GM and its OnStar subsidiary entered into a settlement with the FTC, prohibiting them from sharing some kinds of driver data with third parties. The settlement was finalized this January. That agreement banned the two companies from sharing geolocation data or driver behavior data for five years. At the time, GM also discontinued Smart Driver across its entire range. Now the automaker has reached terms with the District of Columbia and 35 states after their attorneys general joined together to sue GM as well. Read full article Comments

title: Hackers steal $6.3 billion from Binance in record crypto heist
abstract: Binance has suspended all withdrawals after the world’s largest cryptocurrency exchange fell victim to what appears to be the biggest heist in history. The exchange put the “estimated total impact” of the hack at about $6.3 billion and said around $3 billion of affected assets, mainly stablecoins that act as cash for the crypto market, had been frozen. But analysts at Elliptic said the attacker had changed about $3.3 billion into digital assets that could not be frozen and was working to cash those out as traditional currency. title: 2027 Nissan Rogue Hybrid: Drives like an EV, but there's no plug involved
abstract: Nissan provided flights from Washington, DC, to Santa Barbara, California, and accommodation so Ars could drive the Rogue Hybrid. Ars does not accept paid editorial content. Nissan has a new version of its bestselling Rogue SUV, and it’s launching the model here with the latest version of its e-Power hybrid system, which Ars tested in February. Most hybrid cars you can buy today are parallel hybrids, which means that they have an internal combustion engine and an electric motor, both of which drive some or all of the wheels—everything works in parallel. But there’s another approach. Instead of connecting the engine to the wheels via a transmission, it can act as a generator and charge the traction battery, which in turn powers the electric motor. Since the engine and motor work in series, this is known as a series hybrid. That’s mostly how the Chevrolet Volt worked. As does Honda’s hybrid CR-V . Well, mostly; engineers worked out it was more efficient for those cars' gasoline engines to directly drive the wheels at highway speeds, something that to this day makes a certain subset of hybrid car enthusiasts irrationally angry. If you know anyone like that in your life, send them to wherever the nearest Nissan dealership is, because the 2027 Rogue Hybrid is exactly what they’ve been asking for. Series hybrids Under the hood, with its crisp shut line and slim horizontal lights that give me something of a Range Rover vibe, there’s a 1.5 L, three-cylinder turbocharged direct-injection engine that generates 148 hp (110 kW). It only revs to 5,200 rpm because it’s optimized to charge the battery, not cope with the various loads of an engine connected to a gearbox and the wheels. That also allows the engine to operate at a rather impressive 42 percent thermal efficiency—we would need to look at Formula 1 engines to find higher. Read full article Comments

title: Review: You Can See Everything blurs the view of Elizabeth Holmes' deceit
abstract: In 2015, biomedical entrepreneur Elizabeth Holmes was Silicon Valley's golden girl, lauded as the youngest and richest self-made female billionaire thanks to the company she founded, Theranos, which was valued at $9 billion at the height of its success. Then it all came crashing down when accusations of fraud surfaced about the company's signature blood-testing device, culminating in a sensational trial. Holmes was convicted on four counts and sentenced to 11 years in prison. Holmes is back in the headlines thanks to a new film, You Can See Everything , which depicts the final days before Holmes, having exhausted her appeals , went to prison. Co-directed by Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim , it's a surreal, absurdist piece that has largely been received with gushing enthusiasm and no small amount of hype, with some declaring it the best film of the year. A few contrarian voices have emerged over the past week with much-needed reality checks, but there's no denying the film is destined to be an awards-season darling. Pardon me for joining the buzzkills, but I cannot in good conscience jump on the You Can See Everything bandwagon. Sure, it has its moments, and the second half is highly entertaining, but there's nothing here to warrant all the breathless hyperbole. For all their much-touted access, Oppenheim and Fielder have produced a surprisingly shallow film that runs in circles, yielding very little fresh or novel insight—into Holmes, personally, or much else. title: Rocket Report: Winter is coming for Themis; Cowboy Space adds iron to the fire
abstract: Welcome to Edition 9.17 of the Rocket Report! It's been a while since an American company announced plans for a medium-lift new launch vehicle, but that's what happened this week when a startup named Cowboy Space revealed specs for its Big Iron rocket, named for the classic country-western song by Marty Robbins. I'm a huge fan of the name. Maybe Cowboy Space is striking while the iron is hot as the space industry frets over demand for launch outpacing supply. However, Cowboy Space lags far behind so many other launch providers nearing the launch pad with their medium-class rockets, and the company didn't have much hardware to show at this week's big reveal. In other words, don't mistake style for substance. But we're rocket fans at Ars, and we wish them luck. As always, we welcome reader submissions , and if you don't want to miss an issue, please subscribe using the box below (the form will not appear on AMP-enabled versions of the site). Each report will include information on small-, medium-, and heavy-lift rockets as well as a quick look ahead at the next three launches on the calendar. Virgin's new rocket plane reaches home port . The first of Virgin Galactic's new Delta-class rocket planes left its Arizona factory Wednesday for a trip to Spaceport America in neighboring New Mexico, where it will undergo preparations for a test campaign culminating in suborbital flights to the edge of space, Ars reports . Virgin Galactic expects the craft's first commercial spaceflight to take place "early" in the second quarter of 2027, but like every other projected date in aerospace, this should be taken with a grain of salt. Virgin Galactic halted commercial flights of its previous vehicle, VSS Unity , in 2024. Read full article Comments

title: Reddit is moving to “a logged-in-only experience,” CEO says
abstract: In the future, you won’t be able to use Reddit without logging in. Reddit CEO Steve Huffman confirmed the impending change in a letter (PDF) to shareholders today about Q3 performance. He said that Reddit is shifting “to a logged-in-only experience," adding: Moving to primarily logged-in will ensure our users have the best Reddit experience possible, and can find the content and communities most relevant to them. It is better for our business because we will have more signals for ads targeting, and being logged-in leads to higher engagement generally. It also allows us to protect access to Reddit’s extremely valuable corpus of data, and helps us better adapt to emerging regulations around the world. Huffman also said that the login requirement will help Reddit better retain new users. Read full article Comments

title: Microsoft fixes a Windows 11 annoyance as PC revenue declines
abstract: Microsoft is beginning the rollout of a Windows 11 preview update that finally addresses a persistent power user complaint with the operating system: the right-click menu that obliterated years of muscle memory on command locations and hid others behind an additional click. The timing is notable, as the announcement comes alongside Microsoft's quarterly financial report, which showed a continued decline in the business of selling Windows licenses for new PCs. The preview update, KB5127936 , is cumulative for Windows 11 versions 26H2 and 25H2. The update will be a gradual rollout before eventually moving on to a normal rollout for all Windows 11 devices once it reaches general availability. The highlight of the new update should calm annoyed users who have spent years with custom scripts and services in an attempt to shape Windows the way they would prefer it. Users will get a "customize menu" button that controls what commands appear when they right-click their mouse. Users can toggle built-in commands such as Send To or Create Shortcut on or off, rearrange what appears on the main menu, and control which third-party extensions show up in either the main or submenus. The gripe with the right-click menu had been that Microsoft hid familiar command locations behind a top row of icons while moving other familiar commands under the "Show more options" submenu. Now, Windows users can customize the whole thing around their habits. The original Windows 11 right-click menu is a mess. Credit: Microsoft The new preview also highlights a new Windows feature called Cloud Rebuild, a recovery option that can reinstall Windows 11 directly from the cloud, even when an existing Windows 11 fails to boot. Cloud Rebuild will pull the Windows 11 image and needed system drivers directly from Windows Update. Users will not need a custom recovery image or external media to reinstall Windows. There is an important distinction to note, however. Microsoft classifies Cloud Rebuild as a recovery option, but it behaves more like a fresh Windows install than a repair, as existing applications and files will not be included. Those worried about data security can sanitize entire system drives prior to reinstalling. For a full list of improvements coming to Windows 11, including changes to Xbox mode and settings, you can view the official Microsoft release announcement . Read full article Comments

title: Pentagon IG refuses to investigate Starlink/Starshield slowdown in Ukraine
abstract: The Pentagon inspector general's office declined a request from US senators to investigate restrictions recently imposed on the Ukraine military's use of SpaceX's satellite network. Ukraine, which uses SpaceX's Starlink service and the military version known as Starshield, said earlier this month that military drones lost satellite connectivity when traveling above 161 kilometers per hour (100 miles per hour). The limit was removed after about 10 days. Five Democratic and four Republican senators sent an October 15 letter to Department of Defense Inspector General Platte Moring, asking for a probe into the reported disruptions of Starlink and Starshield. The letter asked, among other things, "whether any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield services were directed, authorized, or implemented by SpaceX, the Department of Defense, or other US government entities; whether such restrictions were consistent with applicable US government contracts, and what actions, if any, the Department of Defense took in response." title: 모두가 함께 성장하는 기술 축제, NAVER Engineering Day 10년의 여정
abstract: 기술은 혼자 완성되지 않습니다. ​ 한 사람이 발견한 문제와 해결 과정이 동료에게 전해지고, 그 경험이 또 다른 시도와 개선으로 이어질 때 조직의 기술은 앞으로 나아갑니다. ​ NAVER Engineering Day는 이런 믿음에서 출발했습니다. 2016년, 실무에서 얻은 개발 경험과 새로운 기술 및 플랫폼을 도입하며 배운 점을 나누는 사내 개발자 행사로 시작해 올해 10주년을 맞았습니다. 그동안 Engineering Day는 발표자가 정리한 지식을 듣는 자리를 넘어, 서로의 경험을 연결하고 각자의 업무 문제를 함께 해결하는 장으로 꾸준히 확장돼 왔습니다. ​ 특히 AI가 특정 직군의 전문 도구를 넘어 일하는 방식 전반을 바꾸기 시작하면서 기술을 나눈다는 말의 의미도 달라졌습니다. 중요한 것은 새로운 도구를 아는 데 그치지 않고, 내 문제에 적용해 보고 막히는 지점을 동료와 함께 풀어 보는 경험입니다. ​ 10주년 Engineering Day는 이러한 변화에 맞춰 전 직군이 함께 온라인 세션, 오프라인 워크숍, AI 오픈 코칭데이로 이어지는 4일간의 여정으로 진행됐습니다. ​ 10년 동안 이어진 동료의 경험 Engineering Day의 중심에는 늘 구성원이 직접 준비한 이야기가 있었습니다. 완성된 기술을 소개하는 데 그치지 않고, 실제 업무에서 마주한 문제와 선택, 시행착오, 그 과정에서 얻은 교훈을 나눴습니다. ​ 주제의 범위도 기술 환경과 함께 넓어졌습니다. 백엔드, 데이터, 모바일을 비롯한 개발 분야부터 AI 도구를 활용한 업무 개선과 협업 방식까지, 서로 다른 역할의 구성원이 각자의 관점에서 경험을 꺼내 놓았습니다. 발표를 통해 한 사람의 경험은 여러 동료가 다시 활용할 수 있는 지식이 됐고, 질문과 대화는 다음 실험의 출발점이 됐습니다. ​ Engineering Day가 10년 동안 이어질 수 있었던 힘은 거창한 구호보다 이 단순한 선순환에 있습니다. 먼저 경험한 동료가 기꺼이 나누고, 다른 동료가 자신의 업무에 맞게 다시 시도하며, 그 결과를 또다시 공유하는 문화입니다. ​ 서로의 경험을 발견하는 온라인 세션 첫날에는 구성원들이 직접 준비한 온라인 세션이 열렸습니다. 발표자들은 성공 사례만 소개하지 않았습니다. 문제를 어떻게 정의했는지, 어떤 선택지 사이에서 고민했는지, 실제 적용 과정에서 무엇이 기대와 달랐는지까지 공유했습니다. 덕분에 참가자들은 익숙한 분야의 지식을 확장하는 동시에 평소 접하기 어려웠던 다른 직무의 문제 해결 방식도 살펴볼 수 있었습니다. ​ 온라인 세션은 기술을 '아는 것'에서 시작하는 단계였습니다. 이어진 프로그램에서는 이 지식을 직접 다뤄 보고 각자의 업무와 연결했습니다. ​ 더 나아가 네이버 내부에서만 그치지 않고, 다음 주 부터 Engineering Day에서 발표된 30여개의 온라인 세션을 D2를 통해서 공개할 예정입니다. ​ 두 손으로 따라하며 내 것으로 만드는 워크숍 ​ 이어서 오프라인 워크숍을 진행했습니다. 참가자들은 설명을 듣는 데 머물지 않고, 준비된 예제와 각자의 과제를 직접 다루며 기술을 적용했습니다. ​ 워크숍에서는 개발자를 위한 심화 기술뿐 아니라 비개발 직군의 AI 협업, 디자이너와 개발자의 연결 등 다양한 역할에서 활용할 수 있는 주제를 함께 다뤘습니다. 같은 도구도 맡은 업무와 해결하려는 문제에 따라 쓰임이 달라졌고, 참가자들은 실습 과정에서 동료와 의견을 나누며 각자에게 맞는 활용 방식을 찾았습니다. ​ 이 과정은 기술 공유의 효과가 좋은 설명만으로 완성되지 않는다는 점을 보여 줬습니다. 직접 실행해 보고, 예상과 다른 결과를 확인하고, 그 이유를 함께 짚어 볼 때 지식은 비로소 자신의 경험이 됩니다. ​ 각자의 경험으로 함께 고민하는 AI 오픈 코칭데이 마지막 날에는 올해 처음으로 AI 오픈 코칭데이를 열었습니다. 온라인 세션에서 개념을 익히고 워크숍에서 실습했더라도, 실제 업무에 적용하려는 순간에는 새로운 질문이 생깁니다. 어디서 시작해야 할지, 문제를 어떻게 나눠야 할지, 현재 방식에서 무엇을 바꿔야 할지 막막할 수 있습니다. ​ AI 오픈 코칭데이는 정해진 강의를 듣는 대신 참가자가 자신의 업무 고민을 가져와 동료 코치와 함께 풀어 보는 방식으로 진행했습니다. 참가자는 문제 상황을 설명하고 직접 도구를 실행했으며, 코치는 정답을 건네기보다 문제를 구체화하고 다음 시도를 설계할 수 있도록 도왔습니다. ​ 코칭 과정에서 배운 사람과 가르치는 사람의 경계도 자연스럽게 흐려졌습니다. 코치들은 서로 다른 접근법에서 새로운 관점을 얻었고, 참가자는 자신의 문제를 말로 정리하고 직접 해결 과정을 밟으며 다음 단계로 나아갈 실마리를 찾았습니다. 한 사람의 질문이 주변 동료의 배움이 되고, 한 사람의 해결 경험이 다시 다른 사람에게 전해지는 순간이었습니다. ​ 다음 10년에도, 기술은 사람 사이에서 이어집니다. 10주년 Engineering Day는 지난 시간을 기념하는 행사인 동시에 앞으로의 기술 공유 방식을 살펴보는 자리였습니다. 발표를 통해 발견하고, 워크숍에서 직접 시도하고, 코칭을 통해 내 문제에 연결하는 흐름은 기술 학습이 일회성 콘텐츠 소비에 머물지 않도록 했습니다. ​ AI 시대에는 도구의 변화가 빠른 만큼 모든 답을 미리 준비하기 어렵습니다. 그래서 완성된 답을 전달하는 것만큼 문제를 함께 정의하고, 시도한 과정을 나누며, 서로의 시행착오를 다음 출발점으로 만드는 일이 중요합니다. ​ NAVER Engineering Day의 지난 10년은 동료의 경험이 조직의 지식으로 이어지는 시간이었습니다. 다음 10년에도 NAVER는 각자의 자리에서 발견한 문제와 배움을 연결하고, 함께 더 나은 해답을 만들어 가겠습니다. ​ D2에서 이어갈 Engineering Day의 다양한 기술 이야기에도 많은 관심 부탁드립니다.

title: 사이드카의 선언적 관리: OpenKruise SidecarSet 도입과 운영
abstract: Kubernetes에서 서비스를 운영하다 보면 메인 컨테이너 옆에 사이드카(sidecar) 컨테이너를 붙이는 일이 흔합니다. 사이드카에는 로그와 메트릭 수집, 프록시처럼 주 기능은 아니지만 같은 Pod 안에서 함께 실행되어야 하는 기능이 포함됩니다. 저희 팀이 운영하는 관리형 데이터베이스 서비스도 DB 인스턴스를 Pod 단위로 실행하고, 그 Pod에 DB 컨테이너 외에 헬스 체크, 메트릭과 로그 수집 등을 위한 사이드카를 함께 둡니다. 이 사이드카들은 DB와 같은 데이터 볼륨에 접근해야 하므로 같은 Pod 안에 있어야 하지만, 라이프사이클은 DB와 다릅니다. DB는 한 번 실행하면 몇 달씩 그대로 운영하는 반면, 사이드카는 기능 추가와 버그 수정, 보안 패치로 훨씬 자주 바뀝니다. 사이드카가 바뀔 때마다 그 변경을 모든 인스턴스에 반영해야 하는데, DB 서비스는 유지한 채 실행 중인 Pod의 사이드카만 바꿔야 합니다. 사이드카는 모든 DB Pod에 붙으므로 이 작업은 인스턴스 수만큼 반복됩니다. 그 결과 반영 시점이 인스턴스마다 다를 수 있고, 사이드카 종류가 여럿이면 버전 조합도 인스턴스마다 제각각이 됩니다. DB Pod는 오래 실행되니 이 상태가 그대로 굳어지고, 어떤 인스턴스에 어떤 버전이 실행 중인지 알려면 Pod를 하나씩 조회해야 합니다. 사이드카 수가 늘수록 형상 관리와 배포, 모니터링이 모두 어려워집니다. 이 글은 Kubernetes 환경에서 사이드카를 운영하는 독자를 대상으로, 사이드카를 선언적으로 관리할 수단으로 OpenKruise SidecarSet을 도입한 이유, SidecarSet의 기능과 동작 방식, 운영하며 알게 된 점을 다룹니다. 사이드카 관리의 어려움: 형상 관리, 배포, 모니터링 사이드카를 관리하려면 사이드카 이미지를 한곳에 선언하는 형상 관리, 선언을 실행 중인 Pod에 적용하는 배포, 결과를 조회하는 모니터링이 필요합니다. 그런데 Kubernetes만으로는 이 세 가지가 모두 어렵습니다. 예를 들어 로그 수집 사이드카의 이미지를 바꾸면, 그 사이드카가 들어간 모든 DB Pod에 같이 적용되어야 합니다. 하지만 Kubernetes에서 사이드카 이미지는 Pod 스펙이나 Deployment, StatefulSet의 Pod 템플릿마다 따로 지정되어 있어서 한 번에 바꿀 방법이 없습니다. Pod 템플릿을 고치면 Kubernetes가 Pod를 다시 만들면서 새 이미지를 적용합니다. 하지만 이 과정에서 DB 컨테이너도 함께 재시작되므로 사이드카를 바꿀 때마다 이 방법을 쓸 수는 없습니다. DB는 그대로 둔 채 사이드카만 바꾸려면 실행 중인 Pod의 이미지를 직접 수정(in-place 갱신)해야 합니다. 이때 kubelet은 이미지가 바뀐 컨테이너만 다시 시작하므로 DB 컨테이너는 영향을 받지 않습니다. 다만 이렇게 수정할 수 있는 컨테이너 스펙은 이미지뿐이고, 수정도 Pod마다 따로 해야 합니다. 사이드카 이미지가 바뀔 때마다 대상 Pod를 찾아 하나씩 고치는 일은 Kubernetes가 해 주지 않습니다. 조회도 같은 한계가 있습니다. Deployment, StatefulSet의 status 에 updatedReplicas 가 있지만 템플릿 기준이므로, Pod에서 직접 바꾼 이미지는 집계되지 않습니다. 반영 여부를 확인하려면 Pod마다 status 에 기록된 이미지를 선언과 하나씩 비교해야 합니다. Kubernetes는 워크로드 단위의 재생성과 Pod 하나의 이미지 교체까지만 제공합니다. 여러 워크로드의 사이드카를 한곳에 선언하고, DB를 유지한 채 실행 중인 Pod에 반영하며, 그 결과를 조회하려면 별도의 수단이 필요합니다. 직접 만들 것인가, 가져다 쓸 것인가 가장 단순하게는 대상 Pod를 순회하며 사이드카 이미지를 패치하는 스크립트를 만들 수 있습니다. 그런데 스크립트는 실행한 순간의 Pod 목록에 패치를 보내고 끝나므로, 패치가 실제로 반영됐는지 확인하고 실패한 Pod에 패치를 다시 보내려면 또 다른 스크립트가 필요합니다. 실행 뒤에 생긴 변화도 마찬가지입니다. 사람이 직접 이미지를 되돌린 Pod나 옛 템플릿으로 새로 만들어진 Pod는 다음 스크립트 실행 전까지 이전 버전으로 유지됩니다. 그림 1. 스크립트 실행 사이의 선언과 실제의 어긋남 갱신이 제대로 끝났는지 확인하는 것도 간단하지 않습니다. kubelet이 이미지를 내려받아 컨테이너를 다시 시작하는 과정에서 내려받기가 실패할 수 있고, status 의 이미지 태그만 봐서는 교체가 끝났는지 정확히 알 수 없습니다. 또 어디까지 갱신되었는지를 따로 관리하지 않으면, 갱신을 실행할 때마다 전체 Pod를 확인해야 합니다. 결국 필요한 것은 한 번 실행하고 끝나는 스크립트가 아니라, 의도한 상태(desired state)를 기준으로 실행 중인 Pod를 계속 비교해 맞추는 조정 루프(reconcile loop), 즉 컨트롤러입니다. 이 루프를 저희가 이미 운영 중인 DB 오퍼레이터(DB 인스턴스의 생성과 운영을 자동화하는 컨트롤러)에 넣는 방법도 있습니다. 하지만 이 경우에도 조정 루프를 오퍼레이터 안에 직접 구현해야 합니다. 이미지를 패치하는 것 자체는 Kubernetes가 제공하므로 간단하지만, 이를 안정적으로 운영하려면 다음 네 가지를 갖춰야 합니다. 완료 판정: kubelet이 컨테이너를 실제로 교체했음을 확인 동시성과 범위 제어: 동시에 교체할 개수와 적용 범위를 정하고, 일시 정지와 재개를 지원 진행 집계: 전체 대상 수와 교체가 끝난 수, 정상 상태인 수를 집계 컨트롤러 운영: 컨트롤러 자체의 배포와 가용성, 장애가 났을 때 클러스터에 미치는 영향 관리 이 문제가 저희 팀에만 국한되지는 않을 것이라고 판단했습니다. Kubernetes에서 사이드카를 두고 서비스를 운영하는 팀이라면 어디서든 마주칠 수 있는 문제이기 때문입니다. 그래서 직접 만들기 전에 기존 해결책을 찾아봤습니다. Istio처럼 Pod 생성 시점에 mutating 웹훅으로 사이드카를 주입하는 구현은 여럿 있지만, 실행 중인 Pod의 사이드카를 선언에 맞춰 갱신하지는 않았습니다. 반면 OpenKruise의 SidecarSet은 이 요건까지 갖춘 것으로 확인했습니다. OpenKruise는 Kubernetes의 워크로드 기능을 확장하는 CNCF(Cloud Native Computing Foundation) 인큐베이팅 프로젝트이고, SidecarSet은 사이드카 컨테이너의 라이프사이클을 메인 컨테이너와 분리해 관리하도록 OpenKruise가 제공하는 CR(Custom Resource)입니다. SidecarSet에서는 새 Pod에 웹훅이 항상 최신 정의를 주입하고, 선언을 바꾸면 컨트롤러가 실행 중인 Pod를 맞추므로, 스크립트 실행 사이에 새 Pod가 이전 버전으로 남는 구간이 생기지 않습니다. 다만 사람이 직접 바꾼 Pod는 이 방식으로도 감지되지 않아 운영 규칙으로 막았습니다. 또 컨트롤러는 자신이 주입한 컨테이너를 이름으로 찾아 그 이미지만 바꾸므로, 같은 Pod의 DB 컨테이너 이미지는 바꾸지 않습니다. 외부 컴포넌트가 늘어나는 운영 부담을 감수하면서도 SidecarSet을 도입한 이유는 SidecarSet이 컨트롤러 운영을 제외한 나머지 기능인 완료 판정, 동시성과 범위 제어, 진행 집계를 이미 갖추고 있었기 때문입니다. SidecarSet의 기능 SidecarSet은 형상 관리, 배포, 모니터링을 각각 CR의 선언, updateStrategy , status 로 제공합니다. 앞에서 정리한 네 가지 요건 중 동시성과 범위 제어는 updateStrategy 가, 진행 집계는 status 가 맡습니다. 완료 판정은 SidecarSet의 동작 방식 에서, 컨트롤러 운영의 부담은 운영에서 주의할 점 에서 다룹니다. 이 글의 동작 설명은 저희가 운영 중인 OpenKruise v1.8.3 기준입니다. 형상 관리: 사이드카 정의를 CR 하나에 CR에는 사이드카 컨테이너의 정의 전체가 들어갑니다. 이미지는 물론 실행 사용자와 capability를 정하는 securityContext , 마운트할 볼륨, 기동 인자와 환경 변수, 포트, preStop 훅(hook)까지 담을 수 있습니다. 주

title: AI 시대의 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생 개발자에게
abstract: 시작하며: 2018년과 2026년 사이의 간격과 격변기의 고민 ​ 2018년에 저는 ' 백엔드 개발자를 꿈꾸는 학생개발자에게 '라는 글을 이곳 D2 블로그에 공유했습니다. 당시 학생 개발자들과의 미트업 행사에서 나왔던 질문과 답변을 정리한 글이었습니다. 그 후 8년의 시간이 흘렀기에 그 글만 노출된다면 학생들에게 현시점에 적절한 정보를 주지 못할까 봐 걱정되었습니다. 그래서 2025년 말 설문으로 질문을 받아 후속편을 작성했습니다. ​ 그동안 저도 경험과 지식을 더 쌓았습니다. 하지만 지금 학생 개발자들이 한 질문에는 답하기가 더 어려워졌습니다. 개발자의 역할과 같은 큰 주제를 묻는 질문이 많았는데, 지금은 AI로 인한 변화가 큰 시기이기 때문입니다. 스스로도 확신이 없는 시기에 이런 글을 쓰는 것이 적절할지 고민도 했습니다. ​ 그럼에도 2018년의 글에 보내 주신 관심에 용기를 얻어서 이 글을 발행합니다. 최근의 경험을 나누고 미래를 함께 상상해 보는 일이 지금 시점에는 더 의미가 있다고 생각합니다. 이 글을 목적지가 명확한 안내서보다는 격변기의 스냅샷 정도로 봐 주셨으면 합니다. 주요 질문과 답변 설문을 통해 들어온 질문들을 비슷한 주제로 모아서 답변을 정리했습니다. [AI 시대와 개발자] 가장 비중이 높은 질문 유형이었고 근본적인 주제이기도 합니다. 이 질문에 먼저 답하지 않고서는 다른 이야기를 풀어 가기가 어려웠습니다. ​ ​ AI 시대에 개발자의 역할은 어떻게 달라졌을까요? 누군가는 AI를 인터넷이나 전기, 불에 비견될 정도의 혁명이라고 말합니다. [1] 2025년부터는 그 주장이 과장이 아니라고 느낍니다. 제가 프로그래밍을 시작한 1989년 이후로 '코딩’이라는 활동에 가장 큰 변화가 왔습니다. AI 코딩 도구가 코드를 추천해 주는 역할에서 나아가 소스 작성, OS 명령 실행 등 사람의 실질적인 대리로 행동합니다. ​ 역사를 돌아보면 기술이 발전하면서 지식 근로자가 하는 일은 이전 시대 관리자의 역할에 가까워졌습니다. 1980년대에 개인용 컴퓨터가 보급되기 전까지 지식 근로자의 작업 공간은 종이였고, 수기로 정보를 처리하는 일에 쓰는 시간의 비중이 컸습니다. AI 시대 전에도 계산, 정보의 형식 변환과 취합 등 컴퓨터가 하는 일의 범위는 꾸준히 늘어 왔습니다. 과거의 실무 일부를 컴퓨터가 하게 되면서 말단의 지식 근로자도 영향력이 큰 의사결정에 많이 관여할 수 있게 되었고 권한도 커졌습니다. ​ CAD 도입 전 General Motors의 기술자들이 작업하는 모습 (이미지 출처: ArchDaily ) 이제는 조직의 말단 작업자는 AI이고 모든 개발자는 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었습니다. 사람은 여러 AI 에이전트에게 업무를 지시하고 결과에 피드백을 줍니다. 아래에 나열한 일들은 전통적인 관리자의 역할이기도 하지만 '작업자’를 'AI 에이전트’로 바꿔서 읽어 본다면 이제는 모든 개발자가 하는 일입니다. ​ 다수의 작업자에게 목표와 배경, 추구하는 가치, 평가 기준을 제시한다. 작업자의 정보 탐색 비용을 줄여 준다. 참조할 정보가 어디에 있는지 알려 준다. 작업자별 역할을 명확히 정의하여 할 일을 분배한다. 작업자별 장점과 투자액(과금액) 수준을 고려하여 각자의 작업에 집중할 수 있도록, 컨텍스트가 과도하게 넓어지지 않고 컨텍스트 전환이 최소화되도록 의사결정자와 작업자 간의 효율적인 피드백 사이클을 구축한다. ​ 관리 업무의 멀티태스킹도 개발자가 적응해야 할 환경이 되었습니다. 에이전트에게 많은 일을 맡기려면 다수의 작업자가 병렬로 일을 진행할 수 있도록 지시를 내리고 결과물에는 빠른 피드백을 주어야 합니다. 작업자마다 컨텍스트를 좁혀 줄수록, 넓은 범위의 맥락을 머리에 올려 두고 빠르게 전환해야 하는 부담은 사람에게 더 크게 돌아옵니다. AI 에이전트와 일하는 형태는 여러 메신저 창을 왔다 갔다 하면서 다수와 병렬로 대화를 이어 가는 관리자의 모습과도 닮아 갑니다. 어떤 순간에는 화면을 어지럽게 전환하면서 게임 유닛에게 작업 지시와 확인, 판단을 쉴 틈 없이 하는 프로게이머와도 유사하게 느껴집니다. ​ 정보를 찾을 수 있는 연결 체계와 필요한 권한을 제공하여 에이전트가 막힘없이 일하도록 하는 일이 중요해지고 있습니다. 부작용을 줄이며 코드를 고치고 빠르게 피드백을 받을 수 있는 아키텍처와 워크플로를 설계하는 일도 핵심 업무가 됩니다. 개발자 경험(Developer Experience)뿐만이 아니라 AI 에이전트 입장에서 얼마나 일을 하기 쉬운지가 생산성을 좌우하게 됩니다. 이는 개발 리더가 다른 개발자들이 일하기 좋은 코드 구조와 작업 절차를 잡아 주는 일과도 유사합니다. 아키텍처와 기술 스택, 구현 방식 같은 기술 의사결정은 여전히 중요합니다. 합리적으로 결정하면 AI 에이전트가 더 안전하고 빠르게 일하고, 그렇지 못하면 오히려 기술부채를 쌓습니다. 예를 들면 모듈 경계가 분명하면 에이전트는 고칠 범위를 좁게 잡지만, 경계가 흐리면 비슷한 코드를 여기저기 복제합니다. ​ 더 상위 수준의 설계까지 AI가 맡는 다음 단계도 이미 시작되고 있습니다. 최근의 코딩 에이전트는 다른 에이전트에게 일을 분배하는 리더 역할까지도 수행합니다. 아키텍처도 AI가 제안하는 방향을 개발자가 수용하거나 근거로 드는 빈도가 높아지고 있습니다. 리더와 아키텍트 역할까지 AI가 가져간다면, 조직 수준의 투자와 리스크 감수를 결정하는 일이 사람의 역할로 남을 것입니다. 앞에서 모든 개발자가 AI 팀의 관리자가 되었다고 말씀드렸는데, 이 단계까지 가면 모든 회사 구성원이 한 번 더 승진을 하는 셈입니다. 조직도상의 개인 기여자도 일하는 형태로는 여러 실무팀의 리더들의 리더가 됩니다. 현실 세계 조직도상의 조직장은 리더들의 리더들의 리더가 되니, 적어도 소기업 경영진의 관점에서 생각하고 결정하는 빈도가 높아질 것 같습니다. 경영진이 투자 대비 사업 성과를 평가하듯, AI 사용료에서 종량제 비중이 높아지면서 한 번의 세션, 한 번의 프롬프트가 주는 부가가치에도 이전보다 신경을 쓰게 됩니다. ​ AI는 지치지 않고 병렬로 일하는 대신 세션이 끝나면 맥락을 잊습니다. 이처럼 사람과 지능의 성격이 다르니 관리하는 방법도 달라야 합니다. 그 차이를 전제하더라도, 관리자의 일하는 방식에 하나의 정답이 없다는 점은 AI와 일하는 방식을 고를 때도 참고가 됩니다. 개발을 모르는 팀장도 팀원들에게 맡기면 결과물은 나오고, 몰라서 더 많이 위임하기에 생기는 장점도 있습니다. 반면 개발을 잘 아는 팀장은 처음부터 올바른 방향을 지시해 시행착오를 줄이기도 합니다. ​ AI 에이전트와 일할 때도 코드를 아는 개발자는 상황에 따라 마이크로매니징과 큰 단위의 위임 중에서 고를 수 있습니다. 이렇게 현미경과 망원경을 오가면서 AI를 감독할 수 있다면 특성과 민감도가 다양한 작업을 안정적으로 수행할 수 있을 것입니다. 제가 아는 뛰어난 개발자 중에서는 수 시간 동안 에이전트가 실행할 업무 정의를 잘하시는 분도 있습니다. 프롬프트를 내린 후에 중간에 나오는 메시지를 하나하나 다 보시면서 에이전트가 일을 어긋나게 수행하는 순간을 바로 잡아내시는 분도 있습니다. ​ ​ AI에게 맡겨도 되는 부분과 개발자가 직접 해야 하는 부분이 있을까요? 실행 능력만 놓고 보면 이제는 AI가 개발자가 하는 대부분의 일을 할 수 있고, 더 잘하는 일도 많습니다. 아무리 AI가 발전해도 할 수 없는 일이 무엇일지를 생각해 보면 이 질문에 오래가는 답을 찾을 수 있습니다. 사람만이 '책임’을 질 수 있습니다. AI 에이전트가 모든 작업을 다 해 준다고 해도 그 소프트웨어를 사용자가 쓰게 하는 결정은 사람이 내립니다. 그로 인해 사용자에게 미친 영향의 책임은 AI에게 지시를 내리고 그 결과물을 최종 승인한 사람에게 돌아갑니다. AI 생성 이미지 ​ 누구나 코드를 만들 수 있게 된 시대에 '개발자’라는 명칭이 앞으로도 쓰인다면, 민감한 시스템의 운영 환경에 코드 배포를 승인하는 사람이라는 의미가 가장 크지 않을까 합니다. 그렇다면 문제를 알아보고 예방할 수 있다는 믿음을 주는 사람에게 그런 권한을 부여하고 '개발자’라고 부를 가능성이 높습니다. 그런 믿음을 주려면 코드의 동작 결과를 검증하고 보장하는 장치와

title: Read, Allocate, Route: Role-Coupled Tokenization for Pixel-Space Generative Transformers
abstract: Pixel-space generative Transformers typically use one token per image patch, so capturing finer detail requires more tokens and makes global attention increasingly expensive. We observe that finer detail does not necessarily require more global communication: low-frequency structure benefits from global exchange, while high-frequency detail can be modeled locally. Based on this insight, we introduce SpecSlot, a pixel-space rectified-flow Transformer that decouples output detail from the length of the global attention sequence. SpecSlot expands each spatial anchor into multiple slots, each assigned a disjoint band of DCT coefficients; this separates anchor density from spectral subdivision. Only the lowest-frequency slot from each anchor participates in global attention, while all slots interact locally. This allows the model to increase spectral detail without enlarging the global sequence. A spatial head further adds a local correction to the spectral prediction, while the generative state, target, and loss remain in pixel space. On ImageNet-256, SpecSlot achieves a comparable final FID to a FLOPs-matched JiT control while converging faster. On ImageNet-512, it improves FID by 2.84 over the control with 3.9% fewer FLOPs, and comes within only 0.69 FID of JiT-B/16 at 38.2% lower cost. On text-to-image generation, SpecSlot surpasses JiT-B/8 on DPG-Bench by 1.06 at 40.6% lower forward cost.

title: Retrieval as Traversal: Value-Indexed Memory for Stateful Long-Context Agents
abstract: Long-context models repeatedly solve closely related retrieval problems. Attention or global retrieval can retain large stores, but each forward pass again searches for what matters. Recurrent compression avoids this search only by deciding earlier what information to preserve. Neither mechanism directly exploits that useful memories at neighbouring retrieval steps may substantially overlap. We propose an alternative in which retrieval is a persistent local traversal through an address space. We separate a memory's content from its address.
